After studies in Oxford and in Hamburg, Dominic 
Goodall passed several years working in Pondicherry, 
where he was head of the Pondicherry Centre of the Ecole 
francaise d'Extréme-Orient from 2002 to 2011. He has 
published critical editions of Saiva works and of classical 
Sanskrit poetry (most recently, with Csaba Dezsó, the 
eighth-century Kurtanimata of Dimodaragupta). He is 
currently based in Paris, where he gives lectures on Indian 
and Cambodian Sanskrit literature at the Ecole pratique 
des hautes études (religious science section). 


Après avoir étudié à Oxford et à Hambourg, Dominic 
Goodall a travaillé pendant plusicurs années à Pondicbéry, 
oit il fut responsable du Centre de l'EFEO de 2002 à 2011. 
Il a publié plusicurs éditions critiques d'ouvrages Sivaites et 
poétiques en sanskrit, dont le plus récent, en collaboration 
avec Csaba Dezső, est l'édition ct la traduction anglaise du 
Kuttanimata de Damodaragupta, un roman sanskrit en vers 
du VIIF siecle. Actuellement affecté à Paris, il anime à 
l'EPHE (Ve section) des séminaires de littérature sanskrite 
d'Inde et du Cambodge. 


Alexis G. J. S. Sanderson is a renowned expert on the 
history of Saivism and on tantric traditions. After taking 
undergraduate degrees in Classics and Sanskrit at Balliol 
College, Oxford, he spent six years in Kashmir studying 
with the celebrated scholar and Saiva guru Swami 
Lakshman Joo. From 1977 to 1992 he was Lecturer in 
Sanskrit in the University of Oxford, and Fellow of 
Wolfson College. Since 1992 he has held the Spalding 
Chair of Eastern Religions and Ethics in the University 
of Oxford, and is a Fellow of All Souls College. 


Alexis G. J. S. Sanderson est un spécialiste renommé de 
l'histoire du Sivaisme et des traditions tantriques. Après sa 
formation de premier cycle en lettres classiques et en sanskrit 
au Balliol College, à Oxford, il a passé six ans au 
Cachemire, étudiant auprès du guru Sivaite et lettré réputé 
Swami Lakshman Joo. Maitre de conférences en sanskrit et 
Fellow du Wolfion College entre 1977 et 1992, il occupe 
depuis 1992 la « Spalding Chair of Eastern Religions and 
Ethics » à l'université d'Oxford, où il est Fellow du All Souls 
College. 


Harunaga Isaacson studied in Groningen (MA 1990) and 
was awarded a PhD in Sanskrit by the University of 
Leiden in 1995. After holding positions for research and 
teaching at the Universities of Oxford, Hamburg and 
Pennsylvania, he was appointed Professor of Classical 
Indology in the Department of Indian and Tibetan 
Studies, Asien-Afrika-Institut, Hamburg, in 2006. His 
main research areas are: tantric traditions in 
pre-13"-century South Asia, especially Vajrayana 
Buddhism; classical Sanskrit poetry; classical Indian 
philosophy; and Puranic literature. 


Harunaga Isaacson a étudié à Groningue (MA 1990) et a 
soutenu sa thése de doctorat à l'université de Leyde en 1995. 
Après avoir mené des recherches et enseigné dans les universités 
d'Oxford, de Hambourg et de Pennsylvanie, il occupe depuis 
2006 la chaire d'indologie classique au département des 
études indiennes et tibétaines de l'Asien-Afrika-Institut, à 
Hambourg. Ses centres d'intérét incluent les traditions 
tantriques en Asie du Sud avant 1200, notamment le 
bouddhisme vajrayana, la poésie sanskrite, la philosophie 
indienne classique et les Purana.

L'Institut Frangais de Pondichéry (IFP), UMIFRE 21 CNRS-MAEE, est un établissement a autonomie 
financiére sous la double tutelle du Ministére frangais des Affaires Etrangères et Européennes (MAEE) 
et du Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS). Il est partie intégrante du réseau des 27 
centres de recherche de ce Ministére. Avec le Centre de Sciences Humaines (CSH) à New Delhi, il forme 
PUSR 3330 du CNRS « Savoirs et Mondes Indiens ». Il remplit des missions de recherche, d'expertise 
et de formation en Sciences Humaines et Sociales et en Ecologie dans le Sud et le Sud-est asiatique. Il 
s'intéresse particuliérement aux savoirs et patrimoines culturels indiens (langue et littérature sanskrite, 
histoire des religions, études tamoules..), aux dynamiques sociales contemporaines, et aux ecosystémes 


naturels de l'Inde du Sud. 


The French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP), UMIFRE 21 CNRS-MAEE, is a financially autonomous in- 
stitution under the joint supervision of the French Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs (MAEE) 
and the French National Centre of Scientific Research (CNRS). It is a part of the network of 27 research 
centres under this Ministry. It also forms part of the research unit 3330 "Savoirs et Mondes Indiens? 
of the CNRS, along with the Centre de Sciences Humaines (CSH) in New Delhi. It fulfils its missions 
of research, expertise and training in Human and Social Sciences and Ecology in South and South-East 
Asia. It works particularly in the fields of Indian cultural knowledge and heritage (Sanskrit language and 
literature, history of religions, Tamil studies...), contemporary social dynamics and the natural ecosystems 
of South India.

L'École francaise d’Extréme-Orient (EFEO), fondée en 1900 à Hanoi, est un établissement relevant du 
ministére francais de l'Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche dont la mission scientifique est l'étude 
des civilisations classiques de l'Asie. Son champ de recherches s'étend de l'Inde à la Chine et au Japon 
et, englobant l'ensemble du Sud-Est asiatique, comprend la plupart des sociétés qui furent indianisées ou 
sinisées au cours de l'histoire. Autour de ses dix-sept centres et antennes, installés dans douze pays d'Asie, 
se sont constitués des réseaux de chercheurs locaux et internationaux sur lesquels l'École a pu s'appuyer 
pour construire son essor. L'EFEO aborde l'Asie par des recherches pluridisciplinaires et comparatistes, 
associant l'archéologie, l'histoire, l'anthropologie, la philologie, et les sciences religieuses. À Pondichéry, 
les projets de l'EFEO portent essentiellement sur 1’« indologie » classique : sanskrit, tamoul ancien, 
histoire, histoire de l'art et des religions. 


The mission of The French School of Asian Studies (EFEO), founded in 1900 in Hanoi and today under 
the aegis of the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research, is to study the classical civilizations 
of Asia. Stretching from India, in the West, across the whole of South-East Asia to China and Japan, 
the EFEO’s research areas cover most of the societies which have been ‘Indianised’ or ‘Sinicised’ over 
the course of history. A network of international scholars working at the EFEO's seventeen centres and 
branch offices, which are spread across twelve Asian countries, has been essential in the development of 
the School's research programme. Interdisciplinary projects bring together leading scholars in the fields 
of anthropology, archaeology, history, philology, and religious studies. In Pondicherry, the projects of 
is EFEO focus mainly on classical Indology: Sanskrit, Old Tamil, History, and History of art and of 
religions.

THE EARLY TANTRA SERIES 


Tantric scriptures form the basis of almost all the various theistic schools 
of theology and ritual in post-Vedic India, as well as of a major strand of 
Buddhism (Vajrayana). Among these schools, those centred on the Hindu 
deities Siva and Visnu spread well beyond the Indian subcontinent to Kam- 
buja (Cambodia/Laos/Thailand), Champa (Vietnam) and Indonesia, while 
Buddhist tantrism quickly became pan-Asian. 

With this mini-series, launched within the ‘Collection Indologie’, we 
are releasing some of the fruits of a Franco-German project funded from 
2008 to 2011 by the Agence Nationale pour la Recherche and the Deutsche 
Forschungsgemeinschaft. The series takes its name from the project’s title: 
‘Early Tantra: Discovering the interrelationships and common ritual syntax 
of the Saiva, Buddhist, Vaisnava and Saura traditions? Our aim was to 
study the interrelationships between the tantric traditions on the basis of 
fundamental source-material, which we would edit and publish for the first 
time. For this we made use of some of the exceptionally rich manuscript re- 
sources gathered in the twentieth century and studied by German and French 
research institutes at opposite poles of the sub-continent. 

In recent centuries, the Tamil-speaking South is the only area where a 
vast corpus of Sanskrit texts of what was long the dominant school of tantric 
Saivism continued being copied and so transmitted to the present day. So 
when, in 1956, Jean Filliozat secured a foothold in Pondicherry for French 
indological research, he created an ideal institutional base for the study of 
a forgotten chapter in the religious history of Asia. Gradually, the largest 
specialised manuscript collection of texts relating to the Saiva Siddhanta 
was amassed, recognised in 2005 by UNESCO as a “Memory of the World” 
collection: The Saiva Manuscripts of Pondicherry. 

At the other end of the subcontinent, the cool climate of Nepal has 
preserved ancient manuscripts of texts of virtually every branch of Indian 
learning. Much of the early history of tantrism is thus preserved in the vast 
archive of Nepalese manuscripts microfilmed over more than three decades by 
the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project (NGMPP), then partly 
catalogued by the Nepalese German Manuscript Cataloguing Project (NGM- 
CP), run from Hamburg and from the NGMCP's base in Kathmandu, the 
Nepal Research Centre (NRC). One Nepalese treasure, also included, in 
2019, in UNESCO's register, formed the corner-stone of our project: the 
ninth-century manuscript of the Nisvasatattvasamhita. 

The Early Tantra Series is not a closed collection: as well as the editions 
and translations promised as part of the *Early Tantra” project, studies of 
numerous related works were inspired or further advanced during the project's 
workshops.

ACNOWLEDGEMENTS 


Since this book has been produced by a large team of collaborators, some 
words are required about how we worked and who did what. At the insti- 
gation of Harunaga ISAACSON (Hamburg), a first complete transcription of 
the early manuscript, N, was prepared over a number of years by Dominic 
GOODALL (EFEO), with considerable help at different moments from Pe- 
ter BISSCHOP (then at Edinburgh, now in Leiden) and Diwakar ACHARYA 
(Kyoto). This was collated in a number of places against the apograph K 
and in a very few places against the apograph W. In 2006, Nirajan KAFLE 
(Kathmandu) came to Pondicherry and worked for several months at check- 
ing the transcription of N and collating it systematically against K and W. 
Meanwhile, in 2005 and 2006, an electronic transcription was prepared of 
the three Pondicherry transcripts transmitting the Nisvasakarika, namely 
IFP T.17, 127 and 150 by S. A. S. SARMA, Nibedita ROUT and R. SATHYA- 
NARAYANAN respectively (all of the EFEO, Pondicherry). 

A workshop was then conceived by Alexis SANDERSON (All Souls, Ox- 
ford) and Dominic GOODALL, to which all of the above were invited and 
all came to participate. Along with them came also the following schol- 
ars: Andrea ACRI (Rome/Leiden), Arlo GRIFFITHS (then of Leiden, now 
at the EFEO), Shaman HATLEY (Concordia, Montreal), Kei KATAOKA 
(Fukuoka), Nina MIRNIG (Oxford, Groningen, and now Vienna), and Jun 
TAKASHIMA (Tokyo). A preliminary edition of the text was circulated some 
months before the workshop, which took place at the Pondicherry Centre 
of the EFEO in January 2007, as were the electronic transcriptions of the 
Nisvasakarika. We were happy to have with us also a few other scholars 
who happened to be present in Pondicherry at the time: S. L. P. ANJANEYA 
SARMA (EFEO, Pondicherry), H.N. BHAT (EFEO, Pondicherry), Daniele 
CUNEO (Rome), Hugo DAVID (EPHE), Anil KUMAR ACHARYA (IFP), and 
Deviprasad MISHRA (IFP). 

The plan of the workshop was simple: for two weeks, we would attempt 
to read through and discuss the text and interpretation of as much of the text 
as possible and we would conclude on some afternoons with lectures by the 
participants on the Nisvasa and its bearing on other literature. The reading 


12 Nisvasatattvasamhita 


sessions were chaired by Alexis SANDERSON, who read out each verse and 
proposed an interpretation, which others were then free to discuss. Images 
of the relevant leaves of the old manuscript were projected on a screen for all 
to follow and most participants had computers open to search for parallels. 

In this way, we covered a lot of text and useful suggestions were made 
by many. Thus, although most interpretations were put forward by Alexis 
SANDERSON, who led the discussion, important contributions from relevant 
fields were particularly frequent from Diwakar ACHARYA, Peter BISSCHOP, 
Shaman HATLEY, Anil KUMAR ACHARYA and Harunaga ISAACSON. 

So stimulating and productive was this first meeting of January 2007 
that we were inspired to draw up a three-year project involving the prepa- 
ration of critical editions of a handful of related works structured around 
annual two-week study meetings. To our great delight, the project, entitled 
“Early Tantra: Discovering the interrelationships and common ritual syn- 
tax of the Saiva, Buddhist, Vaisnava and Saura traditions”, was approved 
by the French and German scientific funding institutions, the Agence Na- 
tionale pour la Recherche and the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft. Thus 
with Franco-German financial backing from 2008 to 2011 we were able to 
employ Csaba Kiss and Nirajan KAFLE on the French side, to produce crit- 
ical editions and translations respectively of selected chapters of another 
monumental early Saiva tantric work, the Brahmayamala, and of the intro- 
ductory book of the Ni$vasa corpus, the Nisvasamukha, and on the German 
side we were able to engage Martin DELHEY to edit and translate selected 
chapters of the Manjusriyamulakalpa. 

Our annual reading meetings thereafter—organised by the Nepal Re- 
search Centre in Kathmandu in 2008, the Pondicherry Centre of the École 
francaise d'Extréme-Orient in 2009, and the Asien-Afrika-Institut of the 
University of Hamburg in 2010, and funded from the “Early Tantra” 
project— were therefore further enriched by these dedicated young schol- 
285. and although the meetings were no longer focussed exclusively on the 
Nisvasa, the widening of scope was of immense heuristic value, and drew an 
increasing number of outsiders to the meetings of the project.

SHORT PREFACE 


ON THE IMPORTANCE OF THE NISVASATATTVASAMHITA 
FOR THE HISTORY OF TANTRISM 


Some of the research of recent years that has thrown most light on the ori- 
gins of Tantric Saivism has not been primarily about tantrism proper (the 
Mantramarga, or ‘way of mantras’), but about the non-tantric Paáupata 
religions from which the Mantramarga sprung: the Atimarga. The most 
substantial contribution in this area is an article of SANDERSON that ap- 
peared in 2006 under the title ‘The Lakulas: New Evidence of a System 
Intermediate Between Paficarthika Pagupatism and Agamic Saivism* For 
it is in this article that it is demonstrated that there is a remarkable doctri- 
nal continuity, particularly in the cosmographic conceptions that are set to 
work in the context of religious initiation, between the Atimarga and what 
is arguably the earliest known Saiva tantra, namely the Nisvasa.* 

How may we characterise the shift from Atimarga to the Mantramarga? 
How does the latter set itself apart? The Mantramarga for the first time 
placed strong (perhaps equal) emphasis on two goals: liberation (mukti) and 
the enjoyment of supernatural powers (bhukti). Both goals were attained 
through the power of spells (vidya, mantra), the propitiation and use of 
which required a ritual technology of considerable complexity, and the pur- 
suit of both required initiation (diksa). Now there may seem to be nothing 
very new here: initiation was required for the Atimarga too, and indeed for 
Vedic sacrifices, while the use of mantras for magic is also not an innovation. 
And liberation, after all, is the goal of the Atimarga. But these elements 
have been reconfigured and, in some cases, reinterpreted: the spells of the 
Mantramarga are with five exceptions (the five brahmamantras) not Vedic,” 


*Many of the points made in these opening paragraphs are to be found in GOODALL 
and ISAACSON 2014:124-7. nae 

^Even these exceptions have recently been called into question.The common wisdom 
used to be that the Pasupatas adopted the five brahmamantras from the tenth chapter of 
the Taittiriyaranyaka (see, e.g., HARA 1966*:121). Now ACHARYA (2011:459) has hinted 
at a different but still Vedic origin: “These five mantras are found in the Tuittirzyaranyaka 
(10.43-47), but this may not be the vedic source from which they were first adopted 


Ni$vasatattvasamhita 
16 


and initiation (diksa) is no longer simply a necessary EE ० titi 
a new religion, as it had been for at least the Paficarthika Pasupatas, but 
has become instead a transformative rite. Liberation is no longer brought 
about, as in the Atimarga, through a lengthy progression fa postanitiatony 
practice, but is conceived of as being essentially the resul of the cutting of 
bonds by Śiva, acting through the guru and with mantras as his instruments, 
at the time of initiation. Furthermore, this liberation, conceived of both as 
release from suffering and at the same time as the realisation of omniscience 
and omnipotence, was offered not only to brahmin males, as appears to have 
been the case in the Atimārga, but to those of all varpas and, in some cases, 
to both sexes. 

This combination of innovations may have been a factor in the powerful 
appeal which the Mantramarga evidently had, and in its ability to attract a 
wide base of followers. A similar nexus of notions — mantras as both mag- 
ical and soteriological instruments, to be wielded only by practitioners who 
have received a certain initiation (abhiseka) — also makes its appearance in 
Buddhist tantric sources. 

Crucial evidence for understanding not only the relationship between 
the Atimarga and Mantramarga, as mentioned above, but also between the 
various emerging tantric traditions, is furnished by the Ni$vasa. The last of 
its five sütras, the Guhyasütra, provides evidence of common ground with 
the non-soteriological tantric magic of Buddhist kriyatantras. For, like the 
Marijusriyamilakalpa, it contains a grimoire of recipes in prose for attaining 
magical siddhis. The recipes of both are couched in very similar language, 
with many identical elements identically phrased, and there is at least one 
entire recipe that is the same in almost every detail, as we shall see below. 

Another shared feature that recurs frequently in both sources is the 
notion that three levels of siddhi may be attained by following a given 
recipe, the level attained being heralded by the manifestation of heat, smoke 
or flames. A recipe given in Guhyasütra 10.27ff, for instance, concludes: 
"With oblation one thousand and eight times, power, which is of three [pos- 
sible] grades, arises: if there is heat, power to cover great distances fast 
on foot [is attained]; if there is smoke, the power to disappear; if there are 
flames, the power to fly? These three levels of siddhi are also to be found 


hs क क T Made 55517 a ८। 
by Pasupatas. But, as BISSCHOP had already shown some years earlier (2005:544-5 and 
fn. 101), two of those five brahmamantras, namely AGHORA and TATPURUSA, appear not 
to have been regarded at first by Paáupatas as being even Vedic. Further reflection on 


this theme has been offered by Peter BISSCHOP i i ; :vered in 
Bochum in 2012*. in a still unpublished paper delive 


Short Preface i 
in other Buddhist tantric works, such as the Amoghapasakalparaja,3 but the 
classification is extremely rare in Saiva literature outside the Nisvasa. 

So the Ni$vasa may be linked both to pre-tantric Saiva soteriology and 
to non-Saiva non-soteriological tantric magic found in Buddhist sources. 
It is also linked to some of the tantric literature that was drawn on by 
Kashmirian exegetes of Saiva non-dualism, for a large number of its verses, 
more than a thousand, were adopted and adapted to become part of the 
widely transmitted Svacchanda commented on by Abhinavagupta's disciple 
Ksemaraja in the eleventh century, and the Svacchanda in turn was itself 
cannibalised in a similar fashion by another large esoteric tantra, this time 
of the Trika, namely the Tantrasadbhava. 

Once again, cosmography forms a considerable part of what was adopted, 
but mantras and yogic material have also migrated. The wide influence of 
the Svacchanda, a Bhairava-tantra of the Southern stream (daksinasrotas), 
can be gauged also from its wide dissemination (plentiful manuscripts sur- 
vive today from Kashmir, Nepal and the Tamil-speaking South) and the 
absorption of its ideas into many ritual manuals.* 

Furthermore, the Ni$vasa is an ancestor not only of such tantras, but 
also of the relatively orthodox and Veda-congruent Saivasiddhanta (whose 
scriptures some erroneously refer to as “South Indian agamas", a label which 
rightly belongs only to one relatively late group among them). For although 
the work makes no reference to different schools within the Mantramarga, 
and therefore may well predate a split into Saivasiddhanta, Daksinasrotas, 
etc., it includes what is probably the earliest surviving list of a canon of 
twenty-eight scriptures (Uttarasutra 1:23ff), a list in which its own name 
features, now known as the canon of the twenty-eight principal Siddhanta- 
tantras. It then came to be seen as belonging to the Saivasiddhanta when 
that school came into existence.® 

From the inclusions and omissions in this voluminous work, we can tease 
out a picture of an early stage of development of what appears, judging from 
inscriptions and surviving literature, to have become the dominant strand 
of Tantric Saivism in and beyond the Indian sub-continent by the tenth 
century. Over the last century, various scholars have drawn attention to 
the importance of the Nisvasa, beginning with Hara Prasad SASTRI in 1905 
(1905:Ixxvii and 137-140), and including FARQUHAR (1920:200), BAGCHI 
furnished us with his unpub-

PROLEGOMENA 


The Nisvasa, as has now been suggested several times in print, may be the 
earliest surviving Saiva tantra and its publication is obviously important for 
the reconstruction of an Indian history of ideas. We were therefore anxious 
in 2007 to rush out a preliminary edition with scant annotation, in order to 
be able at once to put some version of the text before interested scholars, as 
soon as we had completed its transcription. But since our access to the text 
is through only one old manuscript, probably of the ninth-century (and three 
twentieth-century copies of that manuscript) the reconstruction of the text 
has proved extremely tricky: the tasks of transcription and interpretation are 
by no means neatly separable, and we have read and reread some parts of the 
text countless times, astonished again and again to discover not only extra 
possibilities of interpretation but also blatant mistranscriptions and slips of 
all kinds. In two cases (in Uttarasutra 5 and Nayasütra 4) we discovered 
extremely late in the day that the foliation, which is not as old as the 
manuscript, had misled us into flipping a folio and so treating a recto as 
a verso. Thus some passages that had seemed destined forever to resist 
all attempts at understanding resolved themselves into sense. We therefore 
came reluctantly to the conclusion in 2009 that to offer a text of the work 
without any translation would be regrettable, partly because we would be 
missing the opportunity ourselves to clarify and improve our interpretations, 
and partly because we wished to help others avoid some of the pointless 


muddles that we had surmounted. 


The early core: the sütras of the Nisvasa 


After this apology for tardiness, let us turn to the text. We have said that 
it is early, but we should add at once that it clearly does not all belong

to the same period. It consists of five books, ordered as follows in the

Mülasütra, and that to this was tacked on, as a form of commentary, the 
Uttarasütra. The Nayasütra was then added on to expand and comment on 
the Uttarasütra. The text was then further expanded by the addition of the 
Guhyasütra, which is by far the largest section of the text. 

The Guhyasütra is less a commentary on the earlier sutras than a sup- 
plement, containing accounts of new subjects, such as the personality-types 
of sadhakas and types of lingas that may be used for siddhi (chapter 1); the 
installation (pratistha) of a linga (chapter 2); accounts of particular siddhis 
and observances (vrata) (chapter 3); a lengthy cosmography (chapters 4-7); 
a variant form of diksa in the form of a series of yagas of the different lev- 
els of the cosmos (chapter 8); the use of mantra-systems other than those 
given in the earliest books, including the VYOMAVYAPIN (chapters 9-11), 
the five brahmamantras (chapters 12-14), long forms of the angamantras 
(chapter 15) and of a ten-syllable mantra called VIDYA (chapters 16-17). It 
is the Guhyasütra which contains grimoires of magical recipes (kalpa) in a 
prose-style that it shares with certain early Buddhist tantric works, such as 
the Manjusriyamilakalpa.’ It refers in its very last verse (18:15, quoted on 
p.23 below) to another work, the karika, as making up the next sütra of 
the work, and this is presumably a reference to the Ni$vasakarika. But the

than one layer!) Whereas the Mülasütra, Uttarasütra and Nayasütra seem

The dates of composition of the Nisvasakarika and Diksottara, beyond 
that we may assume that they are later than the old ४७१५ > (८५५५५०२ the 
four sütras and the Nigvasamukha, are of course difficult E establish. At 
least part of the Nigvasakarika must be contemporary with at least the final 
lines of the Guhyasütra, as we have seen, 80 We might expect them to belong 
to the same period, in other words the seventh century, the period by which, 
as we shall argue below, the final layers had probably joined the early corpus 
and the four sūtras had thus taken their current shape. We know also, from 
quotations in the Tantraloka, that the Diksottara was known to Abhinava- 
gupta (see GOODALL 1998:xli-xliii, fn. 96). As Dr. Shaman HATLEY has 
pointed out to us, one further piece of evidence that also suggests such a 
relatively early date is that the thirty-ninth chapter of the Brahmayamala 
appears to have drawn on the account of Saiva scripture given in chapter 4 
of the Diksottara. The evidence will be presented in the introduction to the 
forthcoming revised version of his doctoral thesis (HATLEY, forthcoming A).

The Nigvasamukha is a case apart, as we have indicated above: although 
it is transmitted in the early manuscript, it Was Dos conceived as a work 
for promulgating tantric teachings, but rather as an introductory book that 
would present the religious context in which the Mantramarga arose. It 
begins its presentation by dividing religious literature — which is to say all 
religious literature that has some validity from the particular perspective 
of the author of this Saiva work — into five types, laukika (lay devotional 
religion), vaidika, adhyatmika (philosophy in a Sankhya vein), atimarga and 
mantramarga (1:21):

a|timargam ca mantrakhyam| 1... 


Each of these is then expounded in turn, excepting the last, which is the 
subject of the sutras of the Ni$vasa.25 


The Early Place of the Nisvasa in Tantric Saivism 


It will be noticed that we speak cautiously of the Mantramarga and not of 
“Tantrism” or “Tantra”, for there seems to be little evidence in the Nisvasa 
that tantra had already become privileged as a term for texts of tantric 
revelation. One might attempt to argue that the expression had become or 
was becoming privileged in such a way from some verses, for instance from 
this question of the goddess in Guhyasütra, 4:5: 


adhvanam me mahadeva brühi vistaraso prabho 
adhvanam ca parijfianam Sivatantresu giyate

1:22 and 1:31-2), and we find &ivatantras distinguished from anyatantras

and had probably not yet evolved into a privileged term for revealed tantric 
literature, such a category of revealed literature did exist (see, e.g., Uttara- 
sutra 1:25ff), and the general term used for it in the Nisvasamukha (1:21 and 
4:135-6) was the Mantramarga. 


The Ni$vasa and the Vamasrotas 


There is evidence that the Mantramarga of the Nisvasa predates a split into 
various schools of Tantric Saivism. It is true that the Uttarasütra (1:26f) 
lists the names of a canon of twenty-eight scriptures, including the Ni$vasa 
itself, a list which, with some small differences, is now known as the list 
of names of scriptures of the canon of the Saivasiddhanta. But there is no 
indication in the Ni$vasa that a school of theology and ritual called Saiva- 
siddhanta existed: the list seems to have been a list of works—some or even 
most of them perhaps mythical—belonging simply to an undifferentiated 
Mantramarga. By speaking of the Mülasütra as possibly the earliest surviv- 
ing Saiva tantra and by referring to other works listed in the Uttarasutra as 
possibly mythical we do not mean that the Mūlasūtra was the earliest Saiva 
tantra: its concision, indeed abruptness, seems rather to suggest that it was 
not the one and only text of its genre at the time of its composition. Further- 
more, although the Saivasiddhanta may not have existed, and although there 
is no other evidence in the text for the existence of other tantric schools, 
other schools that we now refer to as tantric might already have been in 
existence. Fragments of a work belonging to another Saiva tantric school, 
the Vamasrotas, have been discovered among folios of a Gilgit MS of the 
sixth century by Alexis SANDERSON and Somdev VASUDEVA,”° plentiful ev- 
idence of the importance of the central divinities of the Vamasrotas, namely 
the four sisters and their brother Tumburu, is furnished in several chapters 
of the Mafijusriyamilakalpa,7 and there is a surviving work of the same 
School, the Vinasikhatantra, which might be of comparable antiquity.

There appear to be only two tubes, Susumna and Ida (Uttarasutra

continuity between the notions of the early Upanisads and the much 
later accounts of that yogic body such as that quoted above, there is 
an important difference: the Upanisads are referring to blood-vessels, 
whereas the nàdis of the yogic body are primarily carriers of breaths,

absence of a central tube in the Uttarasutra might then be regarded 
as less problematic, since the redactor might simply not have had 
Upanisadic notions of blood-carrying tubes in mind, but rather an 
entirely separate notion of wind-channels.

Paleographical archaism 


This title does not refer, of course, to the palaeography of the early ninth- 
century Nepalese manuscript through which the text is transmitted to us, 
but rather to the clues as to the sort of script used by the redactors. For 
in Nayasutra 1:32ff we have an explanation about how the sadhaka is to 
arrange his body or parts of his body to form the shape of each letter of 
the alphabet in turn. Many of the descriptions are unclear or inconclusive, 
but it seems to us that what is described is a Northern Indian alphabet 
type of between the 4th and the 7th centuries AD, and similar to the one 
to which Somdev VASUDEVA has drawn attention in his article about the 
alphabet-goddess Malini (2007). 


Iconographical archaism 


The notion, widespread in the works of the Saivasiddhanta, that the central 
deity Sadasiva is to be visualised as five-faced and ten-armed is absent from 
the sutras of the Ni$vasa. As Judit TORZSOK has suggested,37 four-faced 
central deities in early tantric sources (such as Tumburu in the Vmasikha- 
tantra) seem to have at some point been widely replaced by central five-faced 
ones. Lesser four-faced divinities may remain, but five faces become the de- 
fault for important figures in many tantric Saiva works. This is perhaps the 
result of the influence of the Saivasiddhanta, in which Sadagiva presumably 
came to be regarded as five-faced when the five brahmamantras became

We may note also the absence in the first three sütras of avahana and 
related verb-forms, which are ubiquitous in other tantric literature. The 
first appearances in the Ni$vasa corpus appear to be those in the Guhya-

Other terminological lacunae are suggestive but less certain: the term 
kunda, for example, to describe the fire-pit seems to be absent from the 
Mulasutro, but makes its appearance in the Uttarasutra (2:21). See our note 
on Mulasutra 3:1c-2 below, in which we refer to EINOO’s observations on 
the term in 2005a (pp. 20-23). Before moving to the next heading, we may 
remark in passing that terminological archaisms of this sort are rather hard 
to spot, and so there may be many more staring us in the face that we have 
not noticed, but that they are in any case rather slippery as evidence for 
dating. 


Theological archaism 


Theological archaism is potentially a rather large subject, since one could 
tease out and discuss at length, for instance, the various clues that suggest 
an evolution in soteriology. But this section is intended instead to gather 
together and present a handful of clear-cut theological criteria for placing 
the Nigvdsa early. One intriguing doctrinal subject that is therefore not 
treated here is the Nisvasa’s ambiguous position on what was to become the 
baseline of Saiddhantika theology: philosophical dualism. As we shall $ a 
occasion to remark below (p. 341), we find that the redactors of the sutras 
of the Nisvasa appear not to have seen the need to choose between philolo- 
sophical dualism and non-dualism, perhaps because the issue Hadinot ye 
been raised as a matter of importance in Saiva circles. Moreover, as we long 
ago observed, referring to Uttarasütra 1: 1390 (GOODALL 1998:lviii):

The first of these criteria is, once again, an absence. In the doctrine 
of the Saivasiddhanta, each soul is innately all-knowing and all-powerful, but 
its nature can only be realised by the removal, through a ritual initiation, 
of bonds that fetter it. The idea that embodied souls are fettered by bonds 
(pàsa) has a long history in Saivism. The ancient name ‘Pasupati’, a name 
of Siva that may be translated as ‘Lord of cattle’ or ‘Lord of beasts’, has 
played a réle in speculation about bondage because the element pasu is 
taken to refer to beast-like individual souls, who are all bound by bonds 
(paga). Indeed a number of Saiva works begin their presentations of doctrine 
in terms of these three ‘P’s: pati (‘the Lord’), pasu (‘bound souls’) and 
pasa (‘bonds’). And even in tantras in which these three do not form by 
themselves the list of didactic categories (padartha) into which the cosmos 
is divided, they usually form at least a part of such lists (v. s.v. padartha in 
TAK 3). 

So what are the bonds by which souls are bound? We quote (without the 
footnotes) this succinct summary of the problem of bondage from SANDER- 
SON's useful résumé of developed Saiddhantika doctrine (1992:285-6):

of bondage, in which the soul fails to realize its innate omni- 
me and omnipotence, is not caused by mere ignorance. The 
ignorance that characterises the unliberated is the effect of an 
imperceptible Impurity (malam) that acts on the soul from out- 
side; and this Impurity, though it is imperceptible, is a material 
substance (dravyam). Because it is a substance, only action

(pasuh, anuh) is therefore said to be constrained in its condition 
by four fetters (pasah): (1) Impurity (malam), (2) maya, (3) 
its past actions (karma), and (4) the power of Siva’s will that

But there is no mention in the Nisvasa of the notion of an innate impurity 
(mala, anavamala) that blocks the capacity of each soul other than Siva. 
Such a notion was already crucial to Saiddhantika theology as formulated by 
Sadyojyotih, who was probably active between 675 and 725 AD,43 and who 
is the first systematising theologian of the Saivasiddhanta of whom works 
survive. Sadyojyotih found the notion of mala in the Svayambhuvasüutrasari- 
graha, from which (using 1:17) he was able to draw the doctrine of malapari- 
paka.44 Given the centrality of bondage and, in particular, of the bond of 
impurity (mala or anava-mala), to Saiddhantika doctrine, one expects to find 
it expounded in all Saiddhantika literature. This suggests that the earliest 
three chapters of the Ni$vasa are earlier than the Svayambhuvasutrasan- 
graha, which cannot be placed, as Sadyojyotih's commentary confirms, later 
than the middle of the seventh century. Moreover, as we began to notice in 
January 2007, this “impurity” is entirely missing not just from the Ni$vasa, 
but also from a few other early scriptures of the Siddhanta which appear, 
on other grounds, to be later than the earliest sütras of the Nisvasa: there 
is no trace of mala in the non-eclectic recensions of the Kalottara (Dvisati- 
kalottara, Sardhatrigatikalottara, Saptasatikakalottara, etc.), in the surviving 
chapters of the Rauravasitrasangraha and of the Nigvasakarika or in the 
Sarvajnanottara.45 In other words, at least one generation of scriptural

Nigvasa. Widespread in tantric Saivism is a set of five (sometimes four) 
indefinable entities called kalas. Their names are nivrtti, pratistha, vidya, 
éanti and, when there is a fifth, éantyatità. They are so commonly homolo- 
gised with different entities in ritual and in the Siva cosmos that it can be 
difficult to know what they really designate (for various homologisations ac- 
cording to a number of sources see Planches I-VIII in SP 3). In Ratnatraya- 
pariksa 86ff, for example, they are characterised as five modes/activities of 
the subtle sound-matter bindu (binduvrttayah), each of which pervades a 
section of the cosmos: nivrtti corresponds to prthivitattva; pratistha to the 
tranche from water up to and including prakrti; vidya to the tranche from 
purusatattva up to and including maya; Santi to vidyatattva, 1$varatattva, 
and sadasivatattva; and Santyatita to Sivatattva (cf. Tantraloka 11:8-9b). 
Indeed it is as labels for tranches of the universe that the five kalas com- 
monly appear in ritual contexts, because they thus constitute one of the 
six initiatory paths that lead through the cosmos, known collectively as the 
sadadhvan, on which more in a moment.

of Sadasiva; in Nayasütra 3:66-7 they are the four kalas of God as bindu.

Archaism in the realm of social religion 


We should place alongside these telling doctrinal differences the evidence 
that suggests that the Ni$vasa reflects an earlier phase in the evolution of 
the social dimension of the religion of the Mantramarga. 


Absence of social rites We may note first of all that there appears to 
be a near total absence of social ritual. We might not of course expect, in 
a Saiva context, to have rites for births and marriages, but in later Saiva 
scriptures there would be an account of death-rites (the growth of which in 
Saiva sources has been documented by Nina MIRNIG 2010) and there are 
none in the books edited in this volume. In the Guhyasitra there is a single 
reference to death-rites (11:38ab): 


vilomahomam hy antyestya ekasitipadena tu 
vilomahomam ] conj.; vilomaho N (unmetrical) 


This follows on immediately after a brief account of vidyadiksa and mukti- 
diksà using the VYOMAVYAPIN, and so it should perhaps be interpreted to 
mean: “For death-rites the oblations should be performed using the word|s] 
of the eighty-one-word mantra [namely the VYOMAVYAPIN] in reverse order”. 

Whereas later Saiva sources reflect borrowings and modifications and 
inventions in the area of post-mortuary ritual, the sutras of the Nigvasa do 
not. 

A possible conclusion that suggests itself is that the Nisvasa might not 
reflect a heavily institutionalised religion, but rather a young movement that 
Saw itself as a path beyond established social religion leading its adepts to 
the attainment of extraordinary powers and to a state of divinity.

Pointing to a social hierarchy within the religion of the Niévasa. Of d

T-17, PP-906-8, 917) and in other parts of the Nifvasakarika (IFP T.17,

Prolegomena E 


One further clarification may be useful for readers who spot that the term 
samayajna, often a synonym for samayin, appears (with a privative prefix) 
in Mulasutra 1:12. We cannot, however, assume that the term is used as a 
synonym for samayin here, and we should note that the post-initiatory rules 
(samaya) after which the samayin is named are mentioned only after the full 
initiation, the muktidiksa, in Mülasütra 5:24. It seems therefore not unlikely 
that samayajna should be used to refer generically to all initiates, since they 
“know the post-initiatory rules', and not to a particular class among them. 


Absence of an initiation for women, kings and simpletons (nirbija 
diksa) And there is another widespread class of initiate not mentioned in 
this fourfold hierarchical classification that is again strikingly absent from 
the Nisvasa, namely the recipient of a seedless liberatory initiation (nirbija 
or nirapeksa diksa) that requires no post-initiatory ritual activity. Such 
seedless initiations were to be conferred on those judged too busy or too 
incompetent for onerous daily rituals, in other words women, idiots and kings 
(see, for example, Svacchanda 4:87-8 and Kirana 6:11-14 and commentary). 
The initiates referred to in the Nisvasa appear instead all to be sadhakas. 


The absence of initiation names We may observe in passing that no 
procedure is recorded in the sutras of the Nisvasa for conferring initiatory 
names. In other sources, the initiand’s casting of a flower or garland on the 
mandala is used to determine the mantra that will form the first part of his 
initiatory name. The subsequent part of the name, in the earliest texts, is 
simply Siva, e.g., in the Svayambhuvasutrasarigraha (13:8c-9): 


anayec chivasamipyam vastrenacchaditananam 
brüyàt tam praksipasvaitam srajam anga Sivopari 
tatpataveditam®? nama sravyam Sivapadottaram

Slightly later still, name-endings are supposed to vary according to the varna 
of the initiands, as the eleventh-century Somasambhupaddhati describes (see 
samayadiksa 107-109 and BRUNNER's annotation: 1977:97-105), -Siva being 
there reserved for Brahmins, -deva for Ksatriyas and -gana for Vaiáyas.7? 

But in the Nisvasa such a naming practice is not recorded and had per- 
haps not yet come into existence. This could therefore be taken as weak 
supporting evidence for the hypothesis that there was little internal hierar- 
chy of the kind that would probably quickly develop in an institutionalised 
religion organised, for instance, into monasteries (matha), about which our 
text is also silent. This is of course not to suggest that mathas of devotees 
of Siva did not exist (we find mention of them for instance in the account 
of lay religion in the Nisvasamukha in 2:34 and 2:36), but rather that they 
were not a part of the religion of the sutras of the Nisvasa. 

The oldest examples of Saiva initiatory names ending in -$iva known to 
us from the inscriptional record belong to the seventh century and are fairly 
widely spread across the sub-continent.

It is clear then that the witnesses diverge quite widely at this point, and 
this different list of gocaras, which is problematically repetitive, is not one 
attested in scriptures of the Mantramarga. Furthermore, as we have men- 
tioned above, South Indian witnesses, such as T. 32, miss out the allusions 
to gocaras and have Nandikegvara’s speech start instead directly from érüy- 
atam abhidhasyami, as does the ‘edition’ of NARAHARINATHA.75 And this 
does seem rather more natural in view of the fact that in the subsequent 
text of the Sivadharmasastra there does not appear to be a division into four 
forms of the Sivadharma to suit four gocaras, as, for instance, the phrase 
caturvidho hy esa dharmah leads us to expect. 

In short, although there is nothing inherently improbable about the idea 
that ardent followers of the religion taught in the Sivadharmaáastra should 
have received special religious names, a phenomenon common to religious 
movements everywhere, the evidence for it is thin. 


The character of prayascitta We may note also another category of so- 
cial religious teaching which is nearly absent from the Nisvasatattvasamhita, 
namely prayascitta, that is to say rites of reparation and expiation. The ex- 
pression prayascitta does occur in the early corpus from time to time, but 
often without detail of what rites are to be conducted to repair or expiate,’ 

and the problems requiring expiation seem not to be social transgressions.’ 

Elsewhere, in most Saiva scripture from the Svayambhuvasütrasarigraha Om 
wards, we find a large body of reparatory and expiatory rites for what 910 
typically transgressions of rules of social order (eating habits, cleanliness;

social interactions). Some expiatory rules that are attributed to recensions 
of the Ni$vasa are quoted in an anthology of chapters devoted to prayascitta 
in Saiva works compiled by Hrdayasgiva,7® but they are not to be found in 
the early corpus. For a fuller discussion of the evolution of prayascitta in 
the Mantramarga, GOODALL’s introduction to the edition of Trilocanagiva’s 
Prayascittasamuccaya. 


The absence of utsavas The annual ceremonies categorised by some as 
prayascitta, namely the pavitrotsava and damanotsava are also absent in 
the Nigvasa. And finally, just as in other demonstrably pre-tenth-century 
Saiddhantika scriptures, the crowded calendar of temple festivals, utsavas, 
is also conspicuous by its absence in the Nisvasa-corpus. 


In short, the Ni$vasa seems to reflect a religion of spell-masters questing 
for empowerment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). That religion is certainly 
still far distant from the religious world of priests in public temples, such 
as is reflected in, for instance, the Kamika, Karana, Ajitagama and other 
such twelfth- and post-twelfth-century South Indian Temple Agamas, and 
it is probably not yet a socially organised religion housed in monasteries 
or ordered around rich householder gurus (such as is reflected in, for in- 
stance, the Kirana, Matariga, etc., and in the surviving paddhatis). So, 
given that it teaches a religion which, like that of Pancarthika-Pasupatas, 
takes for granted and is parasitic upon the social substrate of brahminism, 
it would perhaps be no surprise to find it silent about pratistha too, as 
Jun TAKASHIMA’s study of pratistha in Agamic sources might lead us to 
suppose. For his conclusion (2005:142) speaks of his “hypothesis that the 
earliest stage of the pratistha ritual is the lingaparigraha”, in other words 
appropriation by a sadhaka of an already existing linga.'9

of pratistha is detailed and complex and is part of the Guhyasütra (chapter 
2), 50 8 full discussion will have to be Postponed, but a few features may 
be mentioned here to indicate ways in which it differs from later accounts 
and a longer treatment of lingapratistha in the early Mantramarga will be 
found in GOODALL forthcoming B. 

We may observe first of all that there appears to be no definition of 
pratistha in the NiSvasa and that it would be difficult to say whether there 
is really any one defining moment in the rituals. One might expect a moment 
in which the linga is instilled with some sort of life force to be identified as 
a central moment. But we find here no jivanyasa (as we find in Soma- 
Sambhupaddhati SP4 2:216) or pranapratistha (as in some late South Indian 
Temple Agamas: see TAK3 ad loc.). Another animating moment in other 
traditions is the nayanonmilana, the opening of the eyes of the image with 
a golden stylus. The linga of course does not have eyes, but this moment is 
often equated (for example by Somasambhu in SP4, 2:177) with the tracing 
on the linga of the lines that suggest the glans of a phallus. Again, this 
is ritually accomplished with a golden stylus. Now the tracing of the lines 
on the linga is included in the Guhyasütra (2:73c—75), but it is noteworthy 
that such an equivalence is not alluded to in the Bodhayanagrhyasesasütra's 
Rudrapratisthakalpa (2.16.1314): 


hiranyena tejasa caksur vimocayet “tejo’si” iti 13 
linge cen nivartate, caksusor abhavat 14 


With the fire of gold he should open the eye, saying “You are fire”. In 
the case of [the installation of a] linga, this is omitted, since there are no 
eyes.

Certainly there is no unambiguous presentation in the Nisvasa of the sliding 
of a stone ring down over the liniga, nor is there mention of an a$vattha- 
leaf-shaped representation of the vulva on the inside of the ring, nor is 
there any mention of the showing of the lingamudra, a gesture that suggests 
sexual intercourse, immediately after this solemn joining of the linga with the 
pindika. I mention these absences particularly since BRUNNER's article "The 
sexual aspect of the linga cult according to the Saiddhantika scriptures" 
points to these features in SP4 to shore up her thesis (1998b:95-96).

Vedic mantras are deployed, and not only for brahmaghosa (the creation of 
auspicious ambient noise), but even for the nyasa (though this label is not

References and borrowings in other literature 
SANDERSON has drawn attention to various early references to the Nisvasa 
when speaking of its having been drawn upon extensively by the redactor 


of the Svacchanda (2001:22-31): 


This work, which is much the largest of the Saiddhantika scriptures, 
seems to have been of little importance when viewed with the perspective 
of the Kashmirian commentators and their successors, since they seldom 
refer to it. But there are reasons to suppose that in earlier times it 
was in the forefront of the tradition. In Cambodia, where later Indian 
developments do not appear to have penetrated, it was the principal 
authority of the Saivas; the Varahapurana speaks of the Siddhanta as the 
teaching of this scripture, as though it knew no other; and the Guhya- 
siddhi of Padmavajra speaks of the teaching of the Siddhanta as following 
either ‘the Kalottara etc? or this text. That the text should have fallen 
into obscurity in later times is not surprising. For it contains, as we shall 
see, features that link it closely with the earlier, pre-Tantric Saivism, t00 
closely, I suspect, for the comfort of the later commentators, who received 
and further moulded a Siddhànta more starkly differentiated both from 
that Saivism and from that of the non-Saiddhantika Tantric systems of 
which the Svacchanda is exemplary.

A. conclusion to the discussion of dating 


None of the external references to the Nsvasa takes us back before the eighth 
century, but, as we mentioned at the beginning of this discussion, we feel 
that the cumulative weight of the various other pieces of what might individ- 
ually have been considered merely suggestive evidence allows us to feel some 
confidence that all four sütras of the Ni$vasa had probably attained their 
present form by the seventh century, before the systematising efforts visible 
to us in the Svayambhuvasütrasangraha and in Sadyojyotih's commentary 
thereon. As for the time that must be allowed to have elapsed between the 
composition of the early kernel, the Mülasutra, and the latest layers, the 
final chapters of the Guhyasütra, this will inevitably be a question of taste.

Prolegomena A 


We think that the two extremes should be separated by at least a century. 
For further fuzzy evidence that points to the later layers, particularly the 
kalpas in prose, of the Guhyasütra being completed by the seventh century, 
see our concluding remarks about magic on p. 84 below. 


The place or places of composition? 


For the earliest three sutras of the text, there is very little evidence indeed 
that could be used to point to a particular place of composition. All that 
can be determined is that they are probably Northern works rather than 
Southern ones. This is suggested by the description of the script that is 
given in Nayasutra 1:31ff, and also, arguably, by some of the irregulari- 
ties of language described below, in particular such Prakritisms as sayojya 
(in Uttarasutra 4:51, 5:14, 5:29, 5:45, and Nayasutra 3:67, 4:5), Damaniga 
(for Damane$a, in Mulasutra 5:14), vagendriya (for vagindriya, in Nayasitra 
2:30 and 3:9), jagi$a (for jagadi$a, in Uttarasutra 1:7) and jagotpatti (for 
jagadutpatti, in Nayasutra 2:84). These are not usages found in the cor- 
pus of Southern Siddhantatantras. The few toponyms, however, such as 
Kailasa (Mulasutra 1:2), have a mythical status that makes them useless as 
geographical pointers. It is only in the next layer of composition, that of 
the Guhyasütra and Nigvasamukha, in which we find a toponym that is nei- 
ther semi-mythical nor simply part of a list, namely Kedara (Nisvasamukha 
3:28 and Guhyasütra 16 passim). But even if we were to make the tentative 
assumption that those parts of the text are likely to have been written near 
Kedara, we could not from that conclude anything about the place or places 
of composition of the earliest three sütras. 


Some remarks on yoga 


Through the above discussion of archaisms and of evidence that might point 
to its being older than other Saiva tantric literature, we have revealed or 
mentioned in passing numerous features of the religious world of the text. A 
Picture has emerged of a group of Saiva enthusiasts who have placed magic 
and soteriology on the same plane: liberation (mukti) and the enjoyment 
of supernatural powers (bhukti) are both goals to be attained through the 
same means, namely the ritual propitiation and manipulation of mine. 
Social religion is largely absent, and that seems to be because the movemen 
recruited from the adherents of a substrate brahmanism that provided the 
rites and values of social religion. The central rituals, taught repeatedly 
in the sütras of the Nisvàsa, each time using different mantra-systems, are 


Í Nisvasatattvasamhita 
T 


the first, vidyadiksa, being a rite for neophytes 
antrasādhana, and the second, nirvànadiksà, a 
d sadhakas that guaranteed liberation. These 
initiations were presumably held to place the followers of the religion of the 
Nisvása above and beyond the laity of social brahmanism. We may assume 
that their ritual obligations were considerable, for although we do not find a 
schedule of daily ritual duties laid out as in a paddhati, the information from 
which one could be extrapolated is clearly there, and there are clues that 
indicate that such a schedule was presupposed.'^' What we have until now 
barely touched upon is the róle of yoga, which is the principal subject-matter 
of the Nayasütra and occupies a large part of the Uttarasutra. For magical 
powers were to be pursued not only through rituals, but also through yogic 
practices. As we would expect for such an early work, the yoga taught is 
not a sort of regimen of virtuosic physical exercises.'?? Good upper-body 
posture appears to be described (in Nayasūtra 4:10 6) and a handful of leg- 
postures (asana) are taught (in Nayasutra 4:4c-16 and 4:105), but any one 
of these may be adopted, for the emphasis is on finding and maintaining a 
comfortable posture (see also 4:106) for meditation. 

Unlike Patafjala yoga, the Nigvasa’s yoga is not divided into eight 
“limbs” (astanga), nor does it spell out at any point the angas that it con- 
tains, but it speaks of itself as teaching at one point (in Nayasütra 4:24) 
an essential “supportless” (niralamba) yoga that goes beyond the yoga of 
six “limbs” (sadangayogavarjitam) or that is without those “limbs”. This 
shows that the redactor of the Nayasütra was aware of an existing sadanga- 
yoga, ^3 and it suggests that he thought of the Nayasütra as building upon 
or transcending that tradition. 

We have remarked that the conception of the yogic body reflected in the 
Ni$vasa is archaic in that it has only two tubes and makes no reference to 
the dvadasanta or to the karaneSas (see p.33 above). But we could also 
emphasise what might have been relatively new features in its time, such 85 
its lengthy tattvajaya, in other words a yogic conquest of the tattvas that 
extends the notion of bhütajaya, ‘conquest of the elements’, that we find in 
Yogasütra 3.43 to reach well beyond the ontological ladder of the Sankhyas 
(see Uttarasütra 5 and Nayasutra 3).

In this tattvajaya, the meditation on each tattva from prakrti onwards 
is to be accompanied by meditation on a sound-element of the NAVATMAN 
that has been taught in Uttarasütra 1:11f to correlate with that particular 
element. Thus in Uttarasütra 5:10 we learn that meditation on prakrti is to 
be accompanied by meditation on the syllable U. Whether this blending of 
visualisation with meditation on mantric bijas other than OM (rather than 
other sorts of mantrajapa) is an innovation we cannot say. One feature 
that seems odd about the matching of mantric-elements with levels is that 
when the tattvajaya begins at the bottom of the cosmos in Nayasitra 3, 
all of the evolutes of prakrti are also assigned the prakrtibija, namely U. 
This means that the visualisations of earth, water, fire, air and ether lack 
something that becomes a widespread distinctive feature in later accounts of 
“meditative fixations” (dharana) on the elements, namely their associations 
with the semi-vowels LA, VA, RA, and YA and with HA respectively. The 
convention of associating the semi-vowels with the elements may nonethe- 
less have existed, for the Mulasutra speaks of an agnibija (in 3:8), which 
we have assumed to refer to RA.!?4 Of the others, vayubija and varunabija 
are explicitly mentioned frequently, but only in relatively high-numbered 
chapters of the Guhyasutra. As for the letter L, it is assigned the la- 
bels mahendra, mahendra and aindra in Guhyasütra 13:51, 15:73, 15:102, 
15:121, 96 but it is once called ksmavarna (in Guhyasutra 15:129), presum- 
ably in the sense of ‘the sound of earth (ksma)’, and once called parthiva (in 
Guhyasütra 15:140). The letter associated with akasa, however seems not to 
be H, but rather M,107 just as it is in Paricaratra sources. 98 As for the letter 
H, it gets instead the names moksada (Guhyasütra 13:131) and hetubhuta 
(Guhyasütra 15:69, 15:85).

context of bhütasuddhi, early Paiicaratra sources speak not of five dharanas 
focussing on the five elements, but of only two, namely dahana and plavana; 
other early Saiddhantika sources speak of four, only the first two of which

The classical Saiva dharanas used in bhütasuddhi, such as we find for 
example in Parakhya 14:33ff, appear in other words to be starting to form 
at the time of the redaction of the Nayasütra, and we can see from Bud- 
dhist accounts, such as that of the Vairocanabhisambodhi, and from those 
of other slightly later Saiva sources, such as Kirana 58 and Sardhatrigati- 
kalottara 2:2-4, that the full set of conventions took some time to settle.*°9 
According to such classical Saiva conventions, which are closely mirrored in 
the Paficaratra,”° the earth is associated with the semi-vowel LA and is to 
be visualised as yellow, square and marked with vajras; water is associated 
with the semi-vowel VA and is to be visualised as white, half-moon-shaped, 
and marked with white lotuses; fire is associated with RA and should be 
visualised as a red triangle marked with flames; wind is associated with YA 
and is visualised as a gray or black disc or hexagon marked with six dots; 
ether is associated with HA and is to be visualised as emptiness marked by 
emptiness. They are to be purified respectively by five, four, three, two and 
one yogic udghatas. In the Nayasütra, however, not only is each element 
assigned the same bija, namely U, as we have just seen above, but shapes of 
mandalas are not prescribed and in only two cases are colours mentioned: 
earth is said to be yellow and wind is said to be ‘whirling with black dust’ 
(Arsnarenvakulah). 

The emergence of one other bijamantra in the context of yogic practice 
may be mentioned in passing, namely the CATUSKALA. If our tentative 
interpretations of the opening verses of Nayasütra 4 are not too far from what 
the redactor intended to express, then this passage speaks of meditation 
involving the visualisation of the graphic form of a seed-syllable, perhaps 
HUMM, that expresses the nature of Sada$iva,"? its four mantra-divisions

(kala) being the four kalas that are nivrtti, pratistha, Santi and vidya (for 
which see p. 42 above). This is interesting for more than one reason: not 
only is it a further instance of the integration of bijamantras into yoga, it 
is also an instance of what appears long to have remained widespread in 
tantric Buddhist practice but that appears soon to have lost importance 
in the 88109 Mantramarga, namely the visualisation of mantric graphemes. 
The same emphasis on the visual aspect of the varpas, which in later Saivism 
cedes entirely to a preoccupation with their sonic aspect, is evident elsewhere 
too in the Ni$vasa, most obviously in Nayasitra 1:32ff (referred to above on 
p. 36), where the sadhaka is exhorted to see the shape of every letter of the 
syllabary in his own body. 

Turning to yogic terminology, the Nigvasa appears also to be among 
the earliest surviving works to use (in Nayasutra 4:110ff) the now ubiqui- 
tous labels recaka, puraka and kumbhaka (and variants of those names) 
for the three principal divisions of breath-control (pranayama). In fact, the 
Nisvasa’s pranayama is not quite the same as this widespread tripartite one, 
for it also includes a fourth stage that it calls suprasanta, which, although 
now little known, can be found in some other early Saiva works, as well as 
in certain Buddhist tantric ones (see our note on Nayasütra 4:113). 

Unless we assume them to be hyperbole, the claims made about the 
rewards of yogic practice (such as, for example, in Nayasütra 4:5) suggest 
that yoga, like diksa, might have been considered to be an independent path 
to liberation. We find no trace, however, of the notion that yoga was one of 
four paths, along with kriya[pada], carya[pada] and jnana[pada], that could 
be followed, together or separately, to attain the liberated state. Indeed the 
four padas are nowhere mentioned, either as upayas and therefore as topics 
that the work must cover (the sense found, for example, in the Kirana), or in 
the apparently later sense of text-divisions devoted to those four topics." 

Yoga, again like diksa (or more precisely the rituals which the sadhaka 
may practise after having received diksa), is of course also a means of access 
to magical powers, for through yogic practices the yogin attains supernatu- 
ral control over his own body and faculties. But while the grimoires of the 
Nisvasa, as we shall see in the next section, contain recipes for such ends 
— disappearance (antardhana), flying (akagagamana), traversing ord pa 
tances fast ( pādapracāra™4)— they add also means to control other objects 
and persons: magical murder, subjugation of others (vastkarana), attain-

Some remarks on magic 


We have referred above to the shared magical universe to be found in early 
Buddhist tantric works, in the Vznasikhatantra and in the Nisvasa, and we 
could compare this with other early non-tantric literature in which similar- 
sounding spells appear, for instance Arthasastra 14. But since this volume is 
primarily concerned with the three earliest sütras of the corpus—a layer of 
composition in which no magical recipes are spelled out, even if we think it 
reasonable to assume that such recipes existed and were presupposed by the 
redactors of the text, as the conception of vidyadiksa suggests—we intend 
to postpone a detailed exploration of this rich subject to our edition of the 
Guhyasütra. Just to give an idea, however, of this magical thought-world, 
we quote below four passages that we have commented upon at considerable 
length in a recent paper (GOODALL and ISAACSON, forthcoming), two drawn 
from the Guhyasitra and two from the Mafijusriyamülakalpa, that furnish 
plentiful examples of shared magical ideas.

Taking menstrual blood and enclosing it in three metals, wrapping it in 
asvattha leaves and reciting the mantra over it ten thousand times, if he 
pops it in his mouth, he can travel a hundred leagues and return quickly 
again before sunset. Taking a king’s sword or, if that is impossible, a 
hero’s sword, or [failing that] one made of puspaloha, cleansing it well 
with the five products of the cow, [he should cover it?] with asvattha

succeed. The supernatural power [that may be attained] is of three kinds 
according to whether heat, smoke or flames manifest themselves. If there 
is heat, then he can cover great distances on foot (padapracara); if there 
is smoke, he may become invisible; if there are flames, he may walk in 
the sky and cross through all the worlds. For such a man is a fully 
realised Vidyadhara; he cannot be opposed anywhere. In a place where 
there is only one Jinga or only one tree, or in a cremation ground, or at 
a confluence of rivers, or in a forest, he should there draw the mandala,

uttering the mantra. That tongue will become his sword; having grasped 
it, he will become a spell-bearer. For he will live as long as moon and 
Stars with nothing to impede his movements.

Since, as mentioned just above, we have discussed these at length elsewhere 
(GOODALL and ISAACSON, forthcoming), we shall not examine and furnish 
parallels for the several shared features here, many of them apparently mak- 
ing their first appearance in early tantric sources (rather than in pre-tantric 
magical recipes such as those of, for example, Arthaéastra 14 and of the 
Atharvavedaparisista). Most will be at once obvious: the wrapping of mag- 
ical substances with three metals, with seven aávattha leaves, the use of à 
magical metal called puspaloha, the use of pellets to be held in the mouth 
(gudika) in order to be able to travel great distances (among other magical 
purposes), the raising of vetalas,!?° oblation into the mouth of a corpse, the 
tongue of the corpse used as a 'sword', the preference (both among Saivas 
and Buddhists) for places in which there is only one linga, the ubiquity of 
magical fire-oblations (one might expect distorted versions of Vedic fire-rites 
to have long been used in magical rites, but homas do not feature in the 
magical recipes of the Arthagastra: cf. the remarks of SANDERSON 2006:193 
on the use of fire in the Mantramarga, quoted below on p. 294), the sadha- 
ka's positioning himself to face the Southern side of the linga or caitya Of 
image, etc.

SOURCES AND EDITORIAL POLICIES 


For the text of the sutras of the Ni$vasa, we know of four manuscripts, 
one being a ninth-century Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript of which the other 
three are early twentieth-century apographs. One might therefore suppose 
that the three apographs could be discarded and that only the readings of 
the oldest manuscript should be reported, since it is the sole independent 
witness to the text and since, when the apographs deviate from it, this can 
only be the result of error or of twentieth-century modifications with no 
basis in an earlier transmission. But since the old manuscript is so often 
damaged around the edges, and since the apographs were all copied at a 
time when the margins were less damaged, and since, furthermore, they 
were independent copies, made by scribes with different habits of mind, it is 
useful now to be able to consult them. We could have reported their readings 
only for those portions where the reading of N, the old manuscript, was 
doubtful or invisible to us, but this would not then have given potentially 
interested readers an idea of the reliability of these witnesses. We have 
therefore recorded the readings of two of the apographs throughout; the 
third apograph, T, proved to be of such poor quality that we abandoned 
including its readings after collating just three chapters, Nayasutra 2-4. We 
have left most of its readings in the apparatus so that some data is available 
that shows how poor it is, but we have not collated it for the Mulasutra and 
Uttarasutra. 


N The old manuscript is preserved in the National Archives in Kathman- 
du (NAK MS 1-277/ vi. Saivatantre 103), but we have worked from 
the black and white microfilm of the NGMPP, Reel No. A 41/4, and 
from printouts and scans of that microfilm. Since the leaves were mi- 
crofilmed with other leaves behind them, there are occasions when it 
is difficult to be sure whether a given akgara actually belongs to a 
leaf beneath the one photographed, and we have therefore sometimes 
also had recourse to a more recent and less sharp set of colour digi- 
tal photographs. This is, on the whole, a remarkably पक

carefully. Generally speaking, the Paramesvara manuscript appears 
to be of rougher workmanship, written less evenly, with three, four or 
five lines to a side, and on leaves that are much less regularly shaped. 
The tops of its letters also lean a little more to the left. In other 
words, the two manuscripts present several differences, but none of 
these seemed to us at first blush to point obviously to the conclusion 
that one must be appreciably older or younger than the other. We 
think them palaeographically similar, but we think that if there is 4 
S MS in date, it may be the manuscript of the Nisvasa that 18 
ter.

Editorial conventions 


We have maintained the conventions used for several earlier editions of Saiva 
works that have appeared in the Collection Indologie in recent years. We 
have attempted to reproduce the fragments of text in the lemmata exactly as 
they are printed in the teztus receptus and the apparatus is fully positive.28 
Each lemma in the apparatus is preceded by the verse number and a letter to 
indicate to which pada it belongs and followed by a lemma sign: |. (A spot 
(०) separates different entries within the same pàda.) There follow the sigla 
of the witnesses which read as printed. Where no witness reads as presented, 
small repairs to the text are marked em|endation|; bolder conjectures are 
marked conj[ecture]. (The difference is of course subjective.) Finally the 
variants are reported, followed by the sigla of the witnesses that give them 
and separated from one another by semicolons. A siglum with superscript ०८ 
(ante correctionem) marks readings of a manuscript before alteration (e.g. 
10००), and a siglum with a Superscript pc marks readings of a manuscript 95 
altered (e.g. N°). A single illegible syllable is signified in the apparatus with 
an anceps symbol: —. Where the scribe has marked a syllable as illegible 
to him, this may be represented in the apparatus with a raised dash e 
imitation of a convention often used in Devanagari manuscripts. In song 
places gaps have been left in the manuscripts and these are signified with 8 
LJ. Where damage to the manuscript prevents us from reading some letter 
the lacuna is signalled with an interrupted line: ---.

On some pages, an additional register of apparatus appears above the 
main one and this extra register reports testimonia and gives information 
about parallel passages in other works. 

Three bracketing conventions that have not been mentioned above in the 
descriptions of the individual manuscripts may be signalled. 


Curly braces (( )) enclose editorial suppletions. 

Plus-marks (+ +) enclose text that can be seen to have been added 
(perhaps sometimes only a few seconds after copying what is not brack- 
eted by plus-marks). 

Crux-marks ( t) enclose text that appears to us to be irreparably cor- 
rupt. 


Editorial policies 


Rather than prepare both a diplomatic transcription and a polished edi- 
tion, which would make for a bulky volume whose extra weight would help 
readers little and would have slowed the editors down considerably;?9 we 
have tried to combine what is required from both into a single edition. This 
means that a certain number of non-standard orthographies are retained as 
they appear in the early manuscript (doubled sibilants, for example, where 
in a modern edition one would expect a visarga followed by a sibilant, a 
homorganic nasal where a modern editor would normally print an anusvara, 
etc.) and yet at the same time the text deviates from what is transmitted 
whenever a conjecture is adopted. With such an approach, total consisten- 
cy cannot easily be attained. At one time we decided therefore to try to 
normalise orthography in line with widespread modern typographical prac- 
tices throughout, for instance by replacing doubled consonants in ligatures 
with semi-vowels with single ones, by replacing double sibilants with visar- 
ga plus sibilant, by replacing some anusvaras with homorganic 3 and 
some homorganic nasals with anusvaras and so forth. But we soon realised 
that such a policy also raised difficulties, for we found that we were often 
not sure whether we were dealing with an orthographic habit or an authorial 
aisa usage. For instance, masculine, accusative plurals regularly appear with 
à final anusvara instead of a final n (e.g. puspam in Mulasutra 1:5b, idhmām 
in Mūlasūtra 3:3c, yajãām in Mūlasūtra 6:18d). Are these all instances of 
an authorial peculiarity? Or are all of them transmissional? Or are only

REMARKS ON PECULIARITIES OF LANGUAGE 


Lists of non-standard ‘aiga’ usages have appeared in the introductions 
to a few editions of tantric works (GOUDRIAAN and SCHOTERMAN 
1988:44-109 for the Kubjikamatatantra; GOODALL 1998:lxv-Ixxx for the 
Kirana; TORZSOK 1999*:xxvi-lxix for the Siddhayogesvarimata; GOODALL 
2004:lxxviii-lxxxvii for the Parakhya); and KISS (forthcoming) for the 
Brahmayamala; but since each text has its own idiosyncracies, the Parakhya, 
for instance, being much closer to standard Sanskrit than is the Brahma- 
yamala, an account of the language of the Nivasa (which would figure some- 
where between the Parakhya and the Siddhayogesvarimata on such a scale) 
is given below. For a more discursive account of a comparable form of aia 
language, the reader is referred to that of TORZSOK. In this less well ordered 
presentation, we have referred in footnotes to discussions of comparable ir- 
regularities in OBERLIES’ A Grammar of Epic Sanskrit (2003). This has 
the incidental advantage of highlighting both the kinds of irregularity that 
are shared with the epics and those that are not.

TRANSLATION OF THE MÜLASÜTRA 


1:1 "The 55 spoke: 
How did the self-born [Lord] teach the supreme, secret Siva-knowledge? 
In what place did the goddess hear it? Out of [your] grace [you should 
tell us]. 


This translation reflects the restitution prasadad vaktum arhasi, but 
the last part of the verse might be conjecturally restored in other ways, 
for instance: prasadac chivabhasitam. 


1:2—3 ‘Nandi spoke: 
All the gods, [headed by] Brahma and Visnu, [and] the Ganas, headed 
by Skanda, the sages, celestial nymphs, Yaksas, snakes, Gandharvas 
and Kinnaras, Daityas, spell-bearers, Siddhas, as well as other in- 
habitants of the citadel [of Siva] (puravasinah) [having seen] the God 
of gods, the teacher of the universe, seated upon a peak of Mount 
Kailasa,...’

1:10—11 ‘The acarya, and the pupil, the ground, the [appropriate] ü 
and the powder (rajah), the incubation (adhivasam), the cmm E) 
mandala and the process of worship—teach [these] o God or a 
[and] initiation that leads to liberation, and the supreme Siva-tattys 
[viz. the mantra], knowing which one becomes free of death? 


In this list of topics, most elements can be recognised and their treat- 
ment later in the text identified, but the element rajah is uncertain, 
We considered interpreting it to mean “[purification of] impurities" and 
taking it to refer to Sauca, which was probably mentioned in passing 
below in 1:20b, but we decided this to be implausible. We now believe 
that it might mean “[the details of the colours for the] powder [used 
for the mandala]". It is true that there appears to be no detailed treat- 
ment below of coloured powders, but the different colours required for 
the mantra are indeed referred to, first in Mulasutra 2:2 and then in 
4:3-4 below. As for the others, we find the treatment of the acarya in 
1:14; of the Sisya in 1:15-16; of the ground (bhū is presumably intend- 
ed as a pratipadika here, but we could consider emending to bhith) in 
1:17-19; of the appropriate time for worship in 1:202; of the incubation 
of the gisya in 3:14; of the caru in 3:10-12b; of the mandala in 414 
; of puja in 2:1-10; of nirvanadiksa in 5:1-26 and of the root mantra, 
or TATTVA in 6:5-15. The last of these could of course be taken i 
mean "true knowledge", for that too is presumably essential for t 
performance of initiation, but cf. Sardhatrisatikalottara 1:5-6.

: LN record that Pingala regarded this vipula as

To cite all the material in the dossier would take us too far from our 
subject, but it is worth summing up STEINER's preliminary conclusion, 
namely that the sa-vipula is regular in Vedic and early Buddhist works, 
but suspicious, at the least, in later texts, especially when not preceded 
by a caesura after the fourth syllable and when, as here, there is just 
one isolated case.2° We could therefore perhaps treat the pada here as 
a na-vipula by considering the syllable before -jnan as laghu (assuming, 
in other words, that the author did not regard the conjunct jn as 
necessarily rendering the preceding syllable heavy).

"When the time of the [first] juncture of the day has been reached, the 
competent man, having performed the necessary [matutinal ablutions] 
(krtakrtyah), well-armoured with the mülamantra and the body-part

This interpretation reflects a conjecture. Two possible restitutions 
have been suggested here: either krtanityo vicaksanah (cf. Jranarat- 
१८००, Madras MS, p.200; Uttara-Kamika 20:1; Isanasivagurudeva- 
paddhati mantrapada 43:56) or krtakrtyo vicaksanah, which has been 
preferred because of the parallel in Svacchanda 3:. If we do under- 
stand krtya to refer to obligatory daily rituals (rather than to ablu- 
tions), then we could take pascat karma samarabhet to mean “he 
should then begin [this special] rite [of initiation]”. In other words, 
we could take krtakrtyah to mean krtanityah and take what follows 
to be naimittika. This is possible, for initiation is going to be taught, 
but the reference to “armouring” oneself with the principal mantras 
is presumably a reference to a process that subsequently came to be 
called sakaltkarana (the expression sakalikrtva in Mulasutra 3:9 ap- 
pears to refer to something else), and that later has the form of a 
ritualised process of identifying oneself with the deity worshipped, 
and this is something that we would expect to precede regular dai- 
ly worship. (Furthermore, if this is not a a n = m 
of nityapüjà, then regular daily worship would p be reque 
the Mülasutra.) Here what is emphasised is not self-identi im R PB 
the deity, but protection by being girt with the mantras o y:

On the offering of samidhs into the fire (rather than their being used

four, one for each of the cardinal directions, and they are the seats 
of four deities, Brahma, Sankara, Visnu and Ananta, going clockwise 
from East to North, or, according to Svacchanda 2:219-21; Brahma, 
Rudra, Visnu, Sadasiva.
