Furthermore we should note that the visualisation in the Ni$vasa is 
not preceded by the stages known to us from other Saiva sources, 
suce carving out the faces (vaktrodghatana), or moistening them 
by besprinkling them (vaktrābhighāra), or of choosing one of the faces 
to inflect the fire rites for Santi, abhicāra or the like (though this is 
perhaps implied by 3:7cd) and fusing the other faces into it so that the 
chosen face alone receives the subsequent oblations (vaktraikikarana). 
Moreover the visualisation, though unclear in most details, is not one of 
a ten-armed and five-faced 5858109, for it is stated to have four arms. 
We do not learn how many faces there are in total, and although we 
have interpreted sitottana-m-ürddhavaktram as having the sense of a 
single bahuvrihi interrupted by m as a vocalic glide, “having his upper 
face white and upturned", we could have interpreted it to mean “with 
his face upwards, white and upturned”. We have not done so because 
the next verse appears to refer to a Western face, which suggests after 
all that there may have been five. But even this is uncertain, because | 
the use of the Western face for oblations actually implies that the 
Western face should be the face that is upturned, and so there may in 
fact only have been four faces. (Cf. our notes on the visualisation of 
Igvara in Nayasutra 3:42f.) 
An oddity in the account of the visualisation of the faces of the Siva-fire 
in Sarvajñānottara 4:59 and in Mrgendrakriyapada 3:7 suggests that a 
four-faced form may have been the early default (cf. the observations 
of TORZSOK 2013). Both texts explain the use of the thirty-eight divi- 
sions (kala) of the five brahmamantras to create the body of the deity, 
and both texts refer to the creation of four faces (vaktracatustayam) 
using TATPURUSA. Both then do add the creation of a fifth face, that

This may be another general statement about fire rites and not one 
specifically about fire-rites in the context of initiation. But it could 
be interpreted to apply to an initiation for an initiand who is seek- 
ing the diksa for a particular purpose, e.g. conquest of enemies. Our 
interpretation of tatah as a temporal "then", assumes that the nitya 
rite should always be performed, and that it may then be followed by 
fire-rites inflected to achieve the sadhaka's goals. 

3:9 ‘Using the root-mantra (tattvena), the six auxiliary mantras and with

There are a number of uncertainties here. To begin with, the damaged 
part could have been restored tattvena tu ca sangena, but it looks as 
though the second of the damaged syllables in N might have been a 
retroflex da, and in that case the only restitution that seems possible 
is tattvena tu sadangena. This is problematic, since, as we shall see | 
below (6:19-20), the text seems really not to have the six angas typical । 
of later tantras (the missing sixth being NETRA). If, therefore, N read | 
sadangena, this might have been a corruption, sadangena being a cliché 

in later literature. Another possibility, as we suggest in our annotation 

on Mülasütra 2:3 above, is that RETAH (raised in 6:16) was treated as 

the sixth aga. A third possibility is that the GAYATRI is here included 

as an angamantra (cf. 6:20 below), even though it is excluded from 

the group of arigamantras in 2:3. In the Dvisatikalottara too we find | 
the same oddity of referring to the body-part-mantras as a group of i 
six even though there seem only to be five explained, and there the i 
number six is attained by the expedient of including the SIVAMANTRA 

(a solution which does not seem to work for our passage):

But the principal problem here is to identify what rite 18 be 
formed. In later literature sakalikarana is used of a practice of iq 
tifying with the deity to be worshipped, a practice that involves E 
stalling the deity's mantras upon one's own body, and it would A 
mally be enjoined before worship rather than after it. And indeed 
something approximating to sakalikarana, though not so labelled was 
enjoined in 1:20 above (see our notes), just before the account of wor 
ship. Nonetheless, it is conceivable that adhvanam is here a corruption 
of atmanam, and that this is after all an injunction to transform the 
worshipper's body into that of the deity by the application of the de. 
ity’s mantras. We could therefore instead translate as follows: “Using 
the root-mantra, together with the six arigamantras and with the five 
brahmamantras, he should transform himself into the Sakala deity, 
and he should block the bonds [of bodily existence] by means of the 
root-mantra.” But if this were a standard sakalikarana, why would it 
be included here after puja and agnikarya and just before the cooking 
of the caru? One possible justification might be that it thus precedes 
the consumption of the caru, a gruel-like concoction which, in pre 
tantric ritual, would normally only be consumed by deities and manes 
(see note on 3:11-12 below). But the allusion to the pasas here would 
seem odd, and we have therefore rejected this interpretation.

There are various problems with assuming that it is the pasasütra 
that is referred to in our text. To begin with, we would expect a 
paSasutra to be prepared for a salvific initiation, in which the soul's 
karman in all levels of the cosmos must be destroyed, and yet the 
following chapter gives a vidyadiksa, which is clearly distinguished 
from the muktidiksa given in chapter 5. This objection might be 
answered either by pointing out that the vidyadiksa too appears to 
raise the soul to a higher level in the universe (see 4:16), and so one 
might expect it to contain a purging of lower levels of the cosmos, 
or by interpreting the adhivasa explained below in this chapter to be 
intended to be something that should precede both a vidyadiksa and | 
a muktidiksa. A more serious problem is that the pasasütra is not a | 
feature of diksa in some other early tantric accounts, and that it is | 
not certain whether or not it is alluded to again in the Milasutra. It | 
is possible, however, that it is alluded to in 4:14-15, in the account 
of vidyadiksa, where some bonds are cut, or that, although it is not 
explicitly mentioned in the account of muktidiksa, the homas that are 
to be performed as part of the purification of each level of the cosmos 
(5:3) involve the oblation in the fire of sections of the pasasutra. 

In favour of our interpretation is that it appears to be what is spelled 
out in the beginning of Diksottara 9, with the difference that tattvena 
bandhayet appears to have been interpreted there to refer to binding 
the thread with the mülamantra after it has been detached from the 
initiand's topknot and big toe prior to adhivasa (97-16): see Appendix

3:11-12b “He should make the caru [using the above ingredients] together

The caru in non-tantric contexts is for gods and manes, but in tantric 
contexts, of which this may be the first known example, the caru is 
often offered to Siva in the main support of worship, then to Siva in 
the fire, and then to [Siva in] the disciples and acarya (cf, e.g. Mr- 
gendrakriyapada 7:47-50, Kirana 18:34, and Vinasikhatantra 19-20, 
all in the context of preparation for adhivasa). Here in the Ni$vasa, 
the third part of the caru is given simply "to sadhakas" (not sepa- 
rately to the éisyas and the acarya), but that is probably simply an 
indication that the term sadhaka had not yet acquired its later sense 
of someone belonging to a class of initiates who, alone, were bubhuksu 
(in contradistinction to the liberation-seeking putrakas and samayins, 
who are absent from the Nisvasa).

As for the element mukti in the name of the mandala, perhaps this 
is used primarily or partly because the same mandala is used in the 
nirvanadiksa. 

Round mandalas are not common, and, as we shall see, this option 
appears at once to be forgotten in what immediately follows. (It is 
taken up again, however, in Uttarasütra 3:10, where it is clear that the 
round mandala is based upon the square one.) The description of the 
drawing of the mandala in this chapter is strikingly simple compared 
with later accounts, and this simplicity could perhaps be considered 
as a mark of its antiquity; but the fact that so many options are 
mentioned plainly suggests that, although the Mülasutra may give the 
earliest tantric account known to us of the drawing of a mandala, it 
certainly was not the first.

4:7 ‘Supreme Siva has two states: beyond mantra, and mantra. And the 
soul is held to be twofold: he whose nature/body is mantra (mantrat- 
ma), and he who is [merely] sentient. 


This verse, which has the air of a parenthetical aside or interpolation, 
is difficult to interpret because it presents a categorisation of Siva and 
of the soul that our text appears not to make use of elsewhere and 
that we have found little used in other tantras. 


The first half of the verse is to be found in the middle of chapter 4 of 
the Matasara (f. 31v), where, in the light of what precedes, one might 
expect accusatives, except that, as in our context, it has the air of an 
explicatory aside, as does the half-line that follows it:

Instead of the above interpretation of the second half of the verse, one

been liberated up to the level of becoming mantras and cetanatma 
would refer to embodied souls in need of liberation, such as ourselves.

4:8 ‘For him [viz. the merely “sentient” soul] the rite of initiation must be 
[performed]: after one has installed the womb in the middle of the 
fire, one should cast Siva's [seminal] emission there, while visualising 
(dhyatva) the sadhaka [i.e. the initiand] to be in [Siva’s] penis.’ 
Unless 4:7 was an early interpolation, the tasya must always have 
been intended to refer back to one or other of the two types of soul 
and we have assumed that it refers to the cetanatman. As the first 
step in initiation, the neophyte must be born anew in the fire. Hence 
the womb, which presumably refers to VAGIÓI (whose mantra is raised 
in Mülasutra 6:17ab), is here placed in the fire, then the semen (the 
mantra of which we know, from 6:16d, to be HAH) 


The parallelism with Vedic upanayana is no doubt deliberate: in UP. 
anayana there is rebirth through the Veda; here the rebirth is in Vagish 
a Saiva ectype of Sarasvati, and thus symbolic of Saiva scripture.

Taking the child out to see the sun and moon (niskramana), which 
unusually appears here before *naming", is sometimes dropped from 
the list of brahminical samskaras (in Saiva works it is not normally 
included, for instance, among the samskaras performed for the fire 
before it receives offerings, an exception being in Netratantra 3:53, 
where it again precedes “naming”), but it is included in a handful 
of Saiva works among samskaras that are to be performed for the 
initiand in the course of initiation (see TAK 3, s.v. niskrama), and 
in one of those passages it appears in the same surprising sequence, 
namely before the naming ceremony (Sarvajnanottara 10:42?!?):

The term vidyadiksa is not much used outside the sutras of the 
Nisvasa, even in the texts closely influenced by them (Nisvasakarika, 
Svacchanda, Tantrasadbhava). What is clear is that it is not a purely 
mental operation and that it is therefore not equivalent to what in 
later works may be called jiianadiksa. According to Ksemaraja (Sva- 
cchandatantroddyota ad 4:483cd: sadhakasyabhiseko’yam vidyadiksa- 
ta uttarah), this initiation is preliminary to an abhiseka to become 
a sadhaka and is so-called because vidya refers to the sakalamantra 
(vidya sakalamantras tatkrtà vidyatmakasadasivapadayojanatma $iva- 
padayojanad anantarabhavini ya diksa, tata uttarah sadhakasyayam 
itidanim eva kathyamanaprakaro 'bhisekah karyah). We think that 
Ksemaraja is right to associate the vidyadiksa with qualification for 
sadhana, but that his notions of the sequence of the rites involved for 
becoming a sadhaka may not be what the redactor of the Svacchanda 


intended, who may rather have had in mind the initiation-structure ° 
the Ni$vasa.

the passage quoted above in our note on 4:12, where it appears m n 
stated to be the rite which makes one a sadhaka. Now it is E d to

the entry-level initiation qualified initiates for mantrasadhana. 


In other words, it now seems to us that vidyadiksa is indeed intended 
to be a preliminary initiation and so to correspond to the later samaya- 
diksa, but it is clearly also at the same time a qualification for sadhana. 
As we shall see, this vidyadiksa is followed in 4४7०-18 with a list of 
things that one should know before beginning religious practice in 
the pursuit of siddhi (Mulasitra 18ef: ...buddhva tu tatah sadhanam 
arabhet), and this enumeration of topics, arguably, corresponds with 
the teaching of the rules of the cult (samaya) that might normally 
follow a samayadiksa. And yet the list of topics that must be known 
appears not to be a list of samayas, whose existence is not mentioned 
until the prayer to Candiga at the end of the muktidiksa (Mülasütra 
5:24). It seems clear from that list, and from other evidence, that 
the vidyadiksa is therefore not simply an initiation for the neophyte 
mumuksu, but a preliminary to the pursuit of siddhis for a bubhuksu, 
comparable therefore, at least in that respect, to what in the later 
tradition is known as the visesadiksa. 


Now the cutting and burning of the thread might seem less logical if 
the initiation is a non-salvific rite for neophytes, assuming that this is 
indeed the rite by which the initiand's karman for each birth at each 
level of the cosmos is magically expended. Such thread-burning would 
fit well, however, in an initiation for a bubhuksu, who would wish 
to have the way cleared for him to moksa but to delay the moment 
of reaching liberation in order to be able to experience other-worldly 
pleasures. This is consistent with the linking of the initiand's soul with 
the second highest level of the cosmos, that of the sakala deity, in 4:16 
below. It is perhaps surprising, though, that the cutting of the thread 
has not been described in any detail: no explicit connection has been 
made with the destruction of the initiand’s karman and the cosmos 
will not be mapped out until the muktidiksa of the next chapter. 


On the basis of such evidence as we have been able to find, we are 
inclined to think that the vidyadiksa is both an initiation for neophytes 
and at the same time an initiation for bubhuksus. We surmise that it

The act of tadana, usually the striking of the initiand by the acarya 
with a flower empowered with the ASTRA, is elsewhere used just before 
the soul is extracted from the body and installed on the thread (see 
TAK3, s.v. tadana). It is said to concentrate the soul in one place 
in the initiand’s body, thus enabling the acarya to lift it out (see 
Somasambhupaddhati SP3 2.3 and BRUNNER’s notes ad loc.) Here 
the pasasitra has been burnt in the fire, and the purified soul is now 
without embodiment, so perhaps the tadana here is for reinserting the 
purified soul in the body. It is not clear, however, how the acarya 
would catch hold of the soul to do this (by performing some sort of 
samharamudra over the fire perhaps?). It may instead be a subsidiary 
part (8788) of the rite of cutting the topknot, since it is apparently 
performed with the same mantra.

The term vratani may refer both to the compulsory initial propitiation 
of the principal mantra known elsewhere (e.g. Guhyasütra 3:30) as the 
vidyavrata, as well as to numerous optional timed religious observances 
that may be undertaken after the completion of the vidyavrata. This 
is the model that might be suggested by Guhyasütra 3, in which 30ab 
tells us 


siddhavidyavratastho hi jape ca vratam arabhet 


Once he has completed the vidyavrata he may proceed to the 
japavrata (?). 


There then follow accounts of a mithyavrata (3:30c-31), a $masana- 
vrata (3:32ab), a ganavrata (3:32c-33b), a lostukavrata (3:33c-34b), 
a kasthavrata (3:34c-35b), a citravrata (3:35c-36b), a vīra- 
vrata (3:36c-37b), a mahavrata (3:37c-38b), and an asidharavrata 
(3:38c-40), without any mention of criteria for choosing between 
them. It is possible, however, that what Guhyasutra 3 instead means 
to teach is that any of those vratas might be chosen as one's vidya- 
vrata. Such a model is rather suggested by parallels elsewhere, such 
as chapter 10 of the Siddhayogesvarimata, which gives instructions for 
numerous options that all appear to satisfy the eee for a 
vidyavrata. Consider also, for example, this instruction from uhya- 
sūtra 10, a chapter devoted to magical rites to be accomplished with 
the VYOMAVYAPIN (10:92):

Having bathed after thus completing his vidyavrata, being fully

Other somewhat later Saiddhantika texts tend not to expound de- 
tailed vratas, with the notable exception of the Matariga (caryapada 
9, for which see SANDERSON 2006:2028). Although the Matariga 
makes having performed one's vidyavrata a prerequisite for being con- 
secrated as an acarya (kriyapada 10:3), it does not make absolutely 
explicit how this may be achieved, and Ramakantha (ad loc.) identifies 
the vidyavrata with the short series of instructions given in kriyapada 
10:4-6 rather than with the Atimarga-derived practices described in 
caryapada 9 (on which no commentary survives). The Sarvajrianottara 
tells us that the officiating guru in a pratistha must have performed his 
vidyavrata (19:3ab: cirnavidyavrato yogi gurudevagnipijakah), and it 
is clear from context that this must refer to the Sivavrata to which 
the preceding six-verse chapter is devoted. No vratas at all are de- 
tailed in the Kirana, in which the old notion of vratacarya has become 
supplanted by carya, conceived of as a body of rules of dress and be- 
haviour for initiates (Kirana 41), that may occasionally be referred to 
with the label vrata (Kirana 6:6). 


No firm conclusion to this digression about the evolution of vratas is 
possible, but it seems likely that in the period of the sutras of the 
Nisvasa each of the various vratas taught could be adopted as the 
vidyavrata, and that we should therefore not interpret vratani to mean 
‘[the vidyavrata and other optional] timed religious observances', but 
rather just ‘timed religious observances’.

in SATHYANARAYANAN's edition]; and cf. Diksottara 17:42cd on p. ion 
of T.17: evam balabalam jüatva atmanasya parasya va), and so it iş 
perhaps more general than siddhyasiddhi-. 


‘Next I shall teach the initiation that bestows liberation; listen from 
me [as I tell it to you] in brief to that [liberation] by attaining which 
men are freed from birth, death, dangers and so forth. Uniting a 
person again [and again] (punah) [with one world after another], the 
expert (matiman) should lift [that person] from one world (tattvat) 
[to the next], beginning with [the world of] Kalagnirudra, up to the 
reality (tattvam) that is free from all defect.’ 


The translation of tattva may seem surprising here, but it is impossible 
that tattva should here have been used in the narrow technical sense 
of tattva of the Saükhyas and later Saivas, for the layers of the cosmos 
here are principally, though not exclusively, bhuvanas. And we shall 
see that the Sankhya tattvasarga (which is neither a tattva nor a bhu- 
vana) is included as a stage on this cosmographic “path”. For this wider 
or vaguer use of tattva in this sort of context, cf., e.g., Nisvasamukha 
4:99, where it is used of the eleven realities of the Lokatitavratas' path. 


We should note, furthermore, that in the cosmography that begins 
here no attempt is made to correlate worlds with tattvas, a tendency 
that we see emerging in the Guhyasütra and that is fully developed 
before the time of the classical Siddhanta of the exegetes: what w° 
have here is rather a stratigraphy of worlds beginning with that of 
Kalagnirudra at the bottom.

a clearer understanding of the 


We have established above (note on Mülasütra 4:14) that the corpus 
of the Nisvasa appears to teach for each mantra-system an initiation 
for the bubhuksu, namely the vidyadiksa, and one for the mumuksu, 
namely the muktidiksa. We left unresolved, however, whether the two 
are conceived of as separate and parallel rituals for initiands with dif- 
ferent goals, or whether muktidiksa is in fact always to be undertaken 
after an initial vidyadiksa. What suggests the latter hypothesis is that 
the muktidiksà is consistently described after an account of the vidya- 
diksa and that the structure of the muktidiksa, if it consists in more 
than the purification of each level of the cosmos (prakriya-Sodhana), 
is never described here or elsewhere in the Nisvasa-corpus. The rites 
that we would expect a salvific initiation to contain (beginning with 
adhivasa) are thus taught only as part of the vidyadiksa and no line 
of text indicates that they must be performed again in the salvific 
initiation. But of course they may have been. 


In short, no certainty is possible here. Even if we knew whether or not 
the initiating priest was expected to weave the ritual elements of the 
vidyadiksa together with the cosmography of the muktidiksa to fashion 
a free-standing ritual of muktidiksa, this would not of course tell us 
whether or not the vidyadiksa and the muktidiksa were performed 
or intended to be performed in close succession. Having emphasised 
that any interpretation is necessarily largely guess-work, mee dita 
interpretation that seems plausible to us: the vidyadiksa probably 
functioned as an initiation for neophytes, who thereby i pae 
for sadhana; this initiation might have been followed S SS 
at a later time by a salvific initiation, the muktidiksa; the A ae is 
was probably never intended to be offered to someone wio 
already received a vidyadiksa. AMOR

The officiant, we are told here, must meditate on the cosmic hier- 
archy (prakriya), make that hierarchy the object of an action un- 
fortunately lost in a lacuna caused by damage to the manuscript, 
and then initiate the candidate through what the text calls the

SANDERSON further suggests (2006:190) that ‘the gnosis of the 
prakriyadhva completes by the time of death the task that initia- 
tion had almost but not completely accomplished’, just as following 
the post-initiatory practices completes the process begun by Agamic 
diksa according to classical Saiddhantika doctrine. (For a discussion 
of how athaSabdanipatah may be understood, we refer the reader to 
SANDERSON 2006:191-192.) 


In the Mülasutro, however, it is made clear how the cosmography 
is ritually involved: the initiand is lifted and placed in each of the 
levels of the cosmos in turn and this involved oblations in the fire 
(note the use of homayitvà in 5:8). SANDERSON therefore con- 
cludes his discussion of Lakula initiation with the following observation 
(2006:192-193): 


Lakula initiation, then, differs from Paficarthika by adding the 
purification of the cosmic hierarchy, so transforming it into a means 
of liberation; and in this most fundamental respect it is one with 
the Agamic Diks&. Details apart, about which we know almost 
nothing in the Lakula case, it differs from the Agamic in only two 
respects. The terminus of its cosmic hierarchy is lower than that 
of the Agamic systems, because those have extended their own 
beyond it in their bid for supremacy within the greater religion; 
and they appear not to have developed the hautri 41158, the w

To conclude, one more trivial and obvious difference between the Laku-

the scant Lakula material available leaves us in doubt about whether

and muktidiksa. And the very use of distinct labels further suggests 
the possibility that the two rites might have been intended to be per- 
formed on separate occasions.

The m after abhasatala is presumably a meaningless euphonic glide 
(inserted after sandhi has been applied to the locative). Because we

ranean paradises (patala) given here (which is the same as that of 
the Guhyasutra) is not shared with other sources: even the Nisvasa- 
mukha (4:106f) gives a different list (see our table on p. 290 above). 
Various lists are presented by GOODALL 2004:289-291, fn. 522.

For another possible instance of such a usage, see 5:132. below.

There is one piece of information that we might have anticipated find- 
ing roughly here and that is conspicuously missing: we might have 
expected to find here an indication of the end of the impure universe 
(as$uddhadhvan) and the beginning of the pure universe Suddhadhvan). 
This division falls just below Vagisvari in the Lakulas' cosmography, 
as we have seen in the annotation to 5:13 above; in the Mantramarga, 
as SANDERSON has pointed out (2006:174-175, Fig. 1), the barrier 
between the pure and impure universes moves up beyond this and is 
often thought to be just above maya: see our table on p. 292 above. 
In the text of the Mülasütra as it now stands, there is no indication 
of such a barrier at this level. Nor do the cosmographical accounts of 
the Guhyasitra (chapters 1 and 7) seem to signal a demarcation here 
between the pure and impure “paths” of the universe, nor does the 
account of Svacchanda 10, nor do some other early sources, such as 
the cosmographical accounts of Svayambhuvasitrasangraha 4, Sarva- 
jrianottara 9 and Kirana 8. But we do find the idea of a split between 
the pure and the impure appearing explicitly in such lines as Kirana 
3:26cd: 


Suddhe 'dhvani givah kartā prokto ‘nanto ‘site prabhuh 
In the pure path Siva is the creator; Ananta is taught to be Lord 
in the impure [path].

mayatmako bhaved granthir aguddhadhvavyavasthitah 


The knot [below the lotus blossom] is maya, which constitutes the 


impure path [of the universe].

pure and the impure, even where an “impure path” is not explic- 
itly mentioned (as it is here in Svacchanda 2:58ab). And this di- 
vision is underlined in some works by stressing that the Section of 
maya below the knot is the adhahputa, a lower half, and the Sec-

the lower puta, and Ksemisa and Brahmapati above it in the upper 
puta. As BAKKER puts it (2000:268), 


[t]he domain that forms the trait d’union between both universes 
is the Mayatattva. According to the Svacchandatantra, this reality 
can be divided into two layers (puta), which are separated by a 
knot or barrier (granthi).

Does this mean that in a yet older Saiva cosmography the barrier 
between impure and pure was the granthi and that this was moved u 
by the Lakulas to above the Rsikula but not at first explicitly aa 
again in the first cosmographical accounts of the Mantramarga? Or 
was the granthi earlier conceived of simply as an almost uncrossable 
point but not a barrier between pure and impure? In that case, the 
idea of such a barrier, introduced perhaps by the Lakulas, might 1 
disappeared in the early works of the Mantramarga before resurfacing 
later. 


Following SANDERSON 2006:174-175, Fig. 1, we have marked in our 
table (p. 292) the point where the Lakula pure universe begins as being 
between Rsikula and Vagisvari, but for Guhyasütra 7 we have instead 
just placed double bars between maya and mahavidya, for we now 
think that the barrier between the pure and impure universes, if it 
was maintained, may have been (once again?) the granthi, which we 
have enclosed with double lines (p. 291). 


The term granthi, apparently identified with maya in Nayasütra 3:36, 
comes in later works to be commonly used as a synonym for maya 
(e.g. Parakhya 4:133 and Mrgendravidyapada 9:1), the barrier between 
pure and impure in classical cosmography, as does the term Gahana, 
the name of 8 world in this same region of the cosmos (see TAK 2, 
s.v. gahana). But it is worth observing that there is no explicit state- 
ment here in the Mülasütra that tells us where maya is situated in the 
cosmos, or indeed whether it is yet a layer in the cosmic hierarchy.

5:22c-23 “On the morrow he should make offerings to Lord Candia, the 


bearer of the axe, together with his five auxiliary mantras, after first 
preparing for him an excellent mandala. He should offer eight hundred 
oblations after offering a prakrantahoma(?)? 


This is one of the earliest surviving references to CandeSa, frequently 
known in early texts as Candiga. He bears, as in his most common 
representation in South Indian temples of all periods, an axe. In echo 
of this, his mandala is usually crescent-moon shaped (e.g. in Kirana 
23:3), though this is not mentioned here. His mantras will be given 
in Mulasutra 6:23-24b below. After initiation, the disciple is to be 
taught the rules of the cult (samaya) before Candesa, who is respon- 
sible for enforcing them, and worship is then offered to Candeása (cf. 
the concluding versions of Kirana 22 in the Nepalese sources?!9). 


For a detailed exposition of what can be known of the history of this 
deity, see GOODALL 2009. 


prakrantahomam hutvà is a problematic expression: it appears to 
mean "having performed the homa that has/had been begun”. Should 
it therefore refer to a homa of Siva that has to be performed before 
that of CandeSa? Perhaps the most likely solution is that the pra- 
krantahoma refers to a basic homa for Cande$a, which is performed 
after worship of Candesa in his mandala, and which must then in turn 
be followed by another homa, also for Candeáa, of either 800 or 108 
oblations, that second homa being inflected for reparation (prayascit- 
ta) of possible shortcomings in the ritual, as the next unit of text, 
5:24-25b, is intended to make clear. As for the number of oblations, 
Satany astau should of course mean 800, but it seems possible that it 
is an aia usage intended to mean 108.

pronoun and an explicit mention of the pasas, which are evidently the 
subject of the next piece of text: "once burnt by initiation, they do 
not rise”. Cf. Suprabheda vidyapada 2:29ab: agnidagdhani bijàni na 
prarohanti bhutale. Cf. also Tantrasadbhava 9:241: 


dagdhabijas tu te devi yesàm diksa tu pasavi 
stabdhah pasa yada tasya tada mokso na saméayah 


We have therefore conjectured that a half-line of text, 5:26ab, has gone 
missing, in which a final statement about the power of diksa might have 
occurred and an explicit mention of the pasas, to supply a subject for 
the following line. For other instances of such similes or metaphors 
involving burnt seeds, see Rauravasütrasangraha 4:51-2, Kirana 6:20 
and Matariga vidyapada 10:30-1. The same idea is present, although 
there is no mention of seeds, in Mrgendra caryapada 25-6:

6:13 "That which is said to be the limit of the ended [breath] one should 
know to be ANTASTHA. It is declared to be unutterable (anuccaryam).

refers to the sound S, the nectareous sound of the incoming breath

in, whereas articulating some sound, at least in theory, necessarily

this verse in his Sardhatrisatikalottaravrtti seems difficult to construe, 
probably because it is corrupt, so we have not quoted it here. He may 
be suggesting that the sound to be produced is HAH (astrabijam eva).

6:25c-26 ‘He should thus (?) form the bijamudra and use it for the throne.

The kotimudra [is used] for dismissing [the deity]? 


Note that Mülasütra 6:26c and 6:26f recur as Uttarasütra 4:23ab. 


The Uttarasitra (4:10ff) gives instructions about how to form these 
mudras. There is, however, no indication later of the function of 
the amrta mudrà, and another mudrà is there added the function 
of which could be understood to be similar, namely the dravyamudra 
(see Uttarasutra 4:15d-18b). But the Uttarasitra’s description given 
of the amrtà reveals that it is what is in later works commonly called 
the dhenumudra, the function of which is often said to be to transform 
the materials used in worship into amrta (see TAK3 s.v. dhenumudra). 
Perhaps the function of this ritual gesture has changed over time?

‘whose essence cannot be articulated’.

1:1-3 ‘In the fifth stream, called the mantra-|stream], is the work known 
by the name of the Mülasütra. |It is of one hundred and fifty plus| 
thirteen 8101085 [in length]. It is spoken of with four names, the first 
being the Mülasütra; the second the Adi-; the third is “The First”; the 
fourth the Pürvasütra. Now that that Sūtra is completed, the second 
Sutra is taught. 


These first 3 prefatory verses link what was probably originally a free- 
standing work, the Mülasutra, with the Uttarasitra. It is possible that 
they were written at the same time as the Uttarasitra, but also possible 
that they were written at some later point with a view to knitting 
together the first two parts of the Ni$vasa corpus. The first might 
actually have been written as a colophon verse to the Mulasutra. It 
locates the Mülasütra in the ‘fifth stream’. This probably refers to the 
classification of 4 ‘streams’ of non-tantric religion that are presented, 
along with a fifth, tantric, stream, the Mantramarga, in Nisvasamukha 
1:21. The second statement is damaged, but it presumably gave the 
size of the Mulasitra to be 163 Sloka-length units ([150]+13). The 
missing pada therefore presumably conveyed the sense ‘150’. A possible 
restitution of 1:1c might be sardham ekaSatan tat tu, except that the 
final syllable, visible at the beginning of the second line of the folio, 
seems really to be ntu. The remaining part of these verses explains that 
the Mülasütra may be referred to by four names: milasutra, pri 
prathamasütra and pürva-sütra and that the Uttarasutra 15 the secon 
sūtra of the Nisvasa. No other sections of text are explicitly referred 
to, and although it is possible that the mention of the fifth ora 
an implicit allusion to the Nisvasamukha (see p. 30), it is E hae 
that the ‘streams’ figured in some other early source now lost to us.

We earlier conjectured tasya Saktih Siva nitya, ‘His Sakti is the eternal

been used here and treated as ending in a short vowel. 


This may not seem to be a very direct response to the question, but 
it is a response nonetheless: Siva does not arise at all, for Siva and his 
Sakti are eternal.

1:13ab ‘These tattvas have been taught to arise from Sadaégiva’ 


This assertion, which echoes 1:7ab, should perhaps not be taken en- 
tirely literally as a statement about the genesis of the Saiva ontolog- 
ical realities. We would not expect Paramaáiva and Sakti to arise 
from Sadasiva; but we must bear in mind that we are talking not 
simply about the tattvas that make up the universe, but we are talk- 
ing about them as correlated with the elements of the NAVATMAN or 
KANTHOSTHYA, which is one of Sadasiva’s eight forms. We must al- 
so bear in mind, however, that the nexus of notions about Sadasiva 
common to the later Saivasiddhanta (see, e.g., Kirana 3:13 and com- 
mentary) have not yet crystallised by the time of the Uttarasutra and, 
secondly, that a clear doctrinal split between philolosophical dualism 
and non-dualism had probably not yet emerged as a fault-line separat- 
ing different tantric schools from each other (see Prolegomena p. 39).

1:19—20 ‘The lord spoke: 


1:21 


At the beginning and end [letters] of the PINDAKSARA [namely the let- 
ters H and U of the NAVATMAN] is to be found the Lord Sadagiva himself 
[namely HU[M], the two letters of which belong to and thus represent 
the first and last of the vargas of the alphabet]. With the NISKALA, 
the SUNYA, the KALADHYA, the KHAMALANKRTA, the KSAPANE KSAYA 
and the ANTASTHA we should connect the [other] six letter[-group]s. 
[Thus] these are [the source of] the eight [letter-]groups with which the 
alphabet (matrka) is taught [to be endowed]? 

We assume that this passage is intended to show how the eight groups 
of letters of the alphabet all derive from the root-mantra of the text. 
Six of those eight groups are linked with six of the eight mantra- 
inflections, and this leaves the first and last of the inflections of the 
root-mantra, namely the SAKALA and the KANTHOSTHYA (or NAVAT- 
MAN) unassigned. We think that the first line might have been meant 
to explain how the first and last vargas of the alphabet emanated from 
the first and last letters of the NAVATMAN, namely H and U, which 
together form the SAKALA. Thus, in fact, all inflections of the root- 
mantra might have been intended to be involved in this demonstration 
that all sound derives from the Siva as mantra.

We take ‘gapam to be a contracted genitive (for "ganànàm) and ye 
have supposed it to act as a plural-marker; but we could Perhaps 
instead interpret it to refer to Siva’s Ganas. 


‘Whoever heard a given tantra, whoever memorised it, that tantra is 
declared to have that person’s name.’ 


Perhaps this means that there were human sages called Kamika, Yo- 
gada (sage), Divya (sage), and so forth, who transmitted the Kamika, 
Yogada, Divya and the others among men. Very different traditions 
about the transmitters of the twenty-eight scriptures may be found in 
later accounts, for which see, for example, GOODALL 1998 appendix 
III. But it seems more likely that these remarks were rather intend- 
ed as a strategy for accounting for subsequent tantras, perhaps ones 
thought of as still not composed at the notional point in time of the di- 
alogue related in the Uttarasütra, and not as commentary on the names 
of the canon of twenty-eight. In other words, this passage seems to 
leave open the way for the integration of such works as the Matang, 
a version transmitted by a particular sage of the Paramesvara, Of the 
Mrgendra, a version of the Kamika. This is not, of course, to Say that 
those particular texts had already been written, but perhaps other 
texts that attached themselves in a similar way to the canon already 
had. Alternatively, one might speculate that this passage, OT pee 


part of it, might have been interpolated in the Uttarasiitra at 8 late 


date.

1:34-6 ‘Siva, Sadagiva, the Vidyesas, Umasuta, the principal Ganas be- 
ginning with Mahakala, Vijaya, Kali, Brahma, Varuna, Vahni, Vayu 
Surya, Candra, Dharma, Indra, and Varuna, along with (?) Ve COR 
Raksasas, and great serpents, and with the Mothers and Guhyakas 
and with the intelligent Garuda—([by them] were studied crores, lakhs, 
billions and hundreds(?) [of granthas of text]. 


If the text is correct here, Siva and Sadagiva are treated as neuter 
perhaps because they are tattvas. Umasuta is not a common name of 
Skanda, whom one would expect to be included among the principal 
Ganas, who are mentioned immediately afterwards, and the text is 
especially insecure here, for the syllables sutah appear within round 
parentheses in K, indicating that they are a conjectural suppletion 
of the scribe. Equally possible would have been to restore umapatih 
(Umapati), who does not appear in the tantravatara of the Diksot- 
tara, unlike Skanda (verse 30c, GOODALL 1998:406), or uma tatha 
(Uma figures as devi in 30b of the same passage). We have hesitated, 
however, to meddle with the text here. 


But in the following pada, we have removed from the text a suppletion 
of K's that seemed to us unlikely: bhairavaé ca ganamukhya. Aside 
from finishing with an unmetrical cadence, this seemed odd to us be- 
cause the text does not refer elsewhere to a person called Bhairava, 
much less to Bhairavas, in the plural. Nonetheless, the initial syllable 
bhai is confirmed by the transcription of W, and so we have conjectured 
bhairavadiganà mukhya and assumed that Bhairava is intended as a 
name for Mahakala, who features in the tantravatara of the Diksottara 
in verse 31 (GOODALL 1998:406). 

We could have retained vijayo, assuming it to be a frozen-sandhi 
form of Vijaya (although who this might be we do not know), but 
in emending to vijaya we have instead chosen to adopt the sugges- 
tion of Shaman HATLEY, who has pointed out (HATLEY forthcoming 
B) that Jaya/Vijaya and Kali occur together in some lists 2 EE 
(e.g. Malinzvijayottara 20:448, Siddhayogesvarimata 20:42cd, dd 
dharmottara 1.41:15cd), that Vijaya may be one of the Mothers or ind i 
(Ur-Skandapurana 64:25), and that Kali (Mahakalt) may be associa 
with the matrs (Ur-Skandapurana 68:8). |

2:1 “The goddess spoke: 
If, o Lord, the syllabary is said to be the greatest mantra, tell [me 
about] the worship of the syllabary; [for] it is from the root that the 
branch grows.’ 


The last pada, in which the atmanepada seems anomalous, appears to 
be an arthantaranyasa: any branch must come from a root (and the 
root of a mantra is in a sense the matrka). Thus mülayaga, in the 
next verse, must mean the same as matrkayaga. We could understand 
yaga here to mean the act of worship (yajanakriya), the pantheon of 
worship (ijyante iti yagah, devata iti yavat), or the place upon which 
the pantheon is installed and worshipped, or all three of these. 
The use of the matrka as mantra is in later literature typically reserved 
for contexts where some general all-purpose mantra is required (hence 
its prominence in the relatively eclectic Isanasivagurudevapaddhati), 
such as in lingoddhara (this appears not to be the context in Diksot- 
tara 9:84ff, for which see Appendix V) or in cases where an existing 
image is to be newly adapted for worship and the mantra that was orig- 
inally installed in it is no longer known. This is made explicit in the 
sadhakabhisekavidhi of Bhoja’s Siddhantasarapaddhati (A, ff. 17-32; 
B, ff. 40v-41r): 
vijfata(vijnata B; jata A)mantrapratisthitalingesu mantran sam-

The half-line 2:15cd is particularly problematic. Both bàna and agni- 
dhaman are names for types of kundas and it is therefore not impos- 
sible that what is transmitted is a corruption involving one or other 
of them. We could therefore, for instance, conjecture agnir bane catur 
yamye purve and interpret ‘Fire, in the case of the bana-type kunda, 
[should be placed] in the South; in the case of the 4-[cornered] type, 
in the East’ (suggestion of Diwakar ACHARYA). But this is somewhat 
unlikely, since only four types were announced and named in 2:12. 


Another possibility might be to leave anirvana§ unchanged and in- 
terpret it as an injunction to the effect that the fire should never be 
allowed to go out (cf. Mrgendrakriyapada 6:31; Prayascittasamuccays 
82-3; Isanasivagurudevapaddhati, prose before kriyapada 15:4); what 
follows might then be expiation if the fire does go out, but the syllables 
caturyamye would remain problematic.

‘(Then follow] the purificatory ( pavitram) preparatory rite for the ghee 
(ajyasamskaram), the heating of the sruva and sruk (sruvadinam) 
and, having performed the preparatory rite for the ghee known as 
the aghara (ajyasamskaram agharya), he should perform the oblations 
known as the ajyabhaga. 


Here we have taken pavitra to be adjectival and we think that the 
purificatory ajyasamskara must be the utpavana, in other words the 
purification of the ghee achieved by skimming its surface with darb- 
ha grass; but we could instead understand it (SASS, SN) to refer to 
the kusa grass itself, which serves as an instrument in performing the 
utpavana (cf. Narayanakantha ad Mrgendrakriyapada 6:33-34: pavit- 
rasya cajyasamskarangasya ... laksanam, ‘the characteristics ... also of 
the pavitra, which is a necessary adjunct of the procedure of purify- 
ing the clarified butter.."). Taking pavitra merely as an adjective may 
seem implausibly weak, since every samskara may have a purificatory 
function; but taking it to refer to blades of darbha grass is also not 
unproblematic, for there appears then to be no verb of which it could 
reasonably the object.

interpret “Having accomplished the purificatory preparatory rite for 
the ghee, the heating of the sruva and sruk and the [remaing rites 
belonging to the(?)] ajyasamskara...”

pidadhyad aparani tu. BRUNNER translates (1998:86): ‘Jl faudra aller 
et venir par la Porte Ouest, et fermer les autres. (Cf. also Sürdha- 
trigatikalottara 7:5, Kirana 28:3; Sarvajrianottara 8:75; Saurasamhita 
8:28.) It is curious that the one direction not mentioned should be 
the East, since that is, in some later literature, the only option men- 
tioned other than the West: thus, e.g., Jianaratnavalt (GOML, p.19): 
vahayet pascimadvaram purvadvaram athapi va. The use of the West- 
ern door may have been originally adopted because of the East being 
conventionally placed at the top, which would mean that someone 
looking down on the mandala would be next to its Western door. The 
later adoption of the option of keeping the Eastern door open might be 
a reflection of mandala-worship having been adapted to or infiuenc 

by temple-worship, given that a large number of temples face East.

4:48 “By means of Sakti he becomes niskala and goes to the Siva-state. 
Alternatively (atha), the acarya may purify [the initiand's rebirths 
throughout] the cosmos (prakriyam) simply (eva) using the cluster-

Instead of performing fire-oblations for each sound in the syllabary as 
a means of purging the soul of all karmic obligation to live through 
future rebirths, the acarya may simply use the letters of the NAVAT- 
MAN, whose correspondences with levels of the cosmos were taught at 
the beginning of the first chapter of the Uttarasutra. The use of the 
syllabary is very lightly touched on here and will be expanded upon 
in the first chapter of the Nayasutra.

“The goddess spoke: 

You have taught the eight varieties of the cluster-letter [mantra], the 
eight [groups of letters] of the alphabet, Sadagiva, Siva and the cos- 
mography.’ 

The ‘eight varieties of the cluster-letter [mantra] are the eight forms 
of the mülamantra (also known as the eight forms of Sadasiva) given 
in Mūlasūtra 6, and in the course of the raising of those forms the 
eight groupings of the alphabet are used. But it is possible that the 
text is here referring back instead to Uttarasūtra 1:18f. A detailed 
cosmographic account occurs in Mulasutra 5, but it is possible that on 
this point the text refers back instead to Uttarasutra 1:13-17.

5:2 "Tell me about Sakti, great lord, and about the yoga of the cosmos 
(prakriyayogam), about what should be aimed at and what should 
not (laksyalaksyam), o lord: on this I have considerable doubt.’ 


As we shall see below, “yoga of the cosmos' could be analysed to 
mean ‘yogic practice involving [levels of] the cosmos’ or "linking oneself 
[through yoga] to [successive levels of] the cosmos’. It is not clear what 
precisely is referred to, among the topics mentioned in the following 
chapter, by the term laksyalaksyam.

Matter, soul, binding fate, time, maya, vidya,

These are the seven tattvas homologised with seven of the ten elements 
of the TATTVA in Uttarasitra 1:10-11. The neuter form dhyatavyanl, 
‘they should be meditated upon’, might have been used because the 
unstated term tattvani is to be understood, but we have assumed 
instead that the neuter adjective is used to qualify the whole group 
of words of various genders. The text now gives an pero uds 
the soul through the cosmic hierarchy to liberation by NET 
Snostic yoga, and in this it seems archaic, harking back to WE a 
intiation (cf. 9. 294): elsewhere in the Mantramarga, 5 e a 
salvific yoga has often been ousted by a more concrete a edd) 
involving fire oblations, with yogic processes (such as ae 
typically retained only as ancillaries to ritual.

5:4-5 ‘Also Sadasiva, who is eight-fold, day, night and the semesters, trans. 

fers, equinox, [a state of awareness in which everything has] the same 
favour as Sakti (Saktisamarasam). Knowing all of these one may reach 
union with Siva. By meditation [upon them] one may attain power; 
omniscience will arise.’ 
With this the programme for the chapter has been announced. Know. 
ing about time must refer to knowing the correspondences between 
macrocosmic external time and microcosmic internal yogic time. One 
might be tempted to repair the metrical fault in 5:4d by emending 
Saktisamarasan (in which both the second and third syllables of the pā- 
da are short) to Saktisamarasyan, but it seems that Saktisamarasa, not 
Saktisamarasya, really is the technical label in this text, and the same 
metrical fault involving the same term recurs in Ultarasutra 5:36d 
below.

nature (tattvadhyanam) [of a given thing]; the second is the meditation

We have puman as an instance of the nominative for an accusative, a

the focus on purusatattva is concluded.

This is one extremely tentative interpretation produced (but not print. 
ed) for the same unit in the Satikakalottara (the fact that both texts 
contain the same string of obscure syllables suggests that there is no 
corruption here). But we may be forcing upon the words an analysis 
that produces a sort of pranava: A-U-M. Perhaps we should rather 
allow Sakti to be some other mantra entirely. If we take trtiye...ayame 
to refer to the third range of consonants (rather than the seemingly 
irrelevant type of breath-stretching known in Nayasutra 4:112 as kumb- 
haka), then we could interpret: “the sixth vowel [with] an anusvara 
and preceded by the second letter in the third range of consonants 
[viz. cH]”. This would give us the mantra CHUM. Perhaps we could 
interpret the irregular compound dvipurvam to mean (irregularly) 
“the second in the first group [viz. KH]”. We could then assume that 
sasthabindukam was tagged on at the end without syntactic mark- 
ers and that the intended mantra was therefore KHUM. No wholly 
convincing interpretation has suggested itself. 


In place of the vocative devi, Satikakalottara has the locative deve: 
this is probably a conscious change, since, as in other recensions of the 
Kalottara, Siva is there addressing Skanda. The bahuvrihi bhinnadehe 
used here as a one-word locative absolute here (cf. Mülasutra 5:26) has 
been unpacked in the Satikakalottara to bhinne dehe.

The cultivation of samarasya has been twice announced using the word 
saktisamarasam (Uttarasutra 5:4, 5:36) and it will be referred to again 
in the same manner in the Nayasütra (4:61); but there seems to be no 
distinction between Saktisamarasa and a state that one might have 
called Sivasamarasa: there appears instead to be just one state of 
samarasya taught in the Uttarasutra and Nayasütra. We may contrast 
this with the Svacchanda, which distinguishes seven levels of samarasya 
(Svacchanda 4:2977c-315), including a saktisamarasya. 


5:44 'Alternatively, with [great] effort resorting to [meditation upon] the 
Supportless [and therefore inconceivable, viz. Siva] upon one's head, 
one should perform worship, recitation, visualisations, [and] all [man- 
ner of religious] acts.’ 


Usually, the supreme form of the divinity cannot be focussed upon by 
the mind at all: cf., e.g., Kirana 3:22c-23.

1:21-22b ‘The letter a stands at the head of all the letters; thus all the 

: letters reside in all the tattvas. It burns all the bonds at the time of

Presumably ‘standing at the head’ of other letters refers both to the 
position of a at the head of the alphabet and to its being present by 
default in each consonant, for the consonants cannot be enunciated 
without pronouncing it. Since the tattvas are in a, and since a is thus 
in the other letters, the tattvas reside therefore in the letters of the 
alphabet.

‘Putting the hands against [the sides of] the body and the shanks next

Presumably this does not, unlike the following descriptions, correspond 
to any written letter. (Indeed one could even understand that this 
refers not to becoming the niskala form of the letter a (a-kara) but a 
niskala shape (akara).) With what follows below, however, we have 
a complete written alphabet described, and thus a much better ba- 
sis for dating on palaeographical grounds than the descriptive names 
offered of the letters in the Jayakhyasamhita (6:32-58), which BHAT- 
TACHARYA in his preface used inventively, but not quite convincingly, 
to date the Jayakhyasamhita to the fifth century (pp.30-35). His 
demonstration fails to persuade because such code-names for the let- 
ters can easily be borrowed from one source to another without change, 
long after the script that suggested the code-names has ceased to be 
used, and this proves indeed to have been the case for a number of 
works later than the Jayakhyasamhita, as a glance at TOKUNAGA’S ar 
ticle of 1990 reveals. More convincing is VASUDEVA'S demonstration 
(2004) that the ordering of the letters of the alphabet deity Malini was 
originally based on the position taken by the letters in a top-to-toe vr 
sualisation of her body in which each letter, because of its distinctive 
written shape in an early Northern alphabet, represented a body-part 
or ornament. In that instance too, however, the identifications of let- 
ters with body-parts is shared by other sources, utm 
and so although the identifications seem old, their appearance In hat 
Malinivijayottara can once again plainly not be used to argue dh 
the composition of the Malinivijayottara must date from the pene D 
Which the script that is implicit in the identifications vig qum A 
the Ni$vasa, however, we do have such evidence: if it were »

7४४४००८. J 
s vasatattvasamhita 


below, most of the descriptions cannot help us to pin down any one 
century or place. 

The descriptions of some letters are unintelligible (several vowels, for 
instance, and the letters kha, jha and fia), and quite a number are 
clear or nearly clear but cannot usefully be used for dating (the letters 
cha, gha and tha, for instance, are too unchanging for too long to be 
useful for our purposes). Among the more interesting cases are ta, dha, 
ma, la and ha (see below). On the basis of these, we can assert with 
confidence that this part of the text was probably written between the 
fourth and the seventh centuries.?34 


Aside from its value for situating the text in time and place, this 
account of the written alphabet is evidence, as we have remarked above 
(see p. 77 above), of the importance of the visual aspect of letters in the 
Saivism of the early Mantramarga: the purpose of adopting with one’s 
body the shape of each grapheme, as will be explained in 1:75c-82b 
below, is to attain liberation and control over all mantras. Emphasis on 
this visual aspect appears to have retained its importance in Tantric 
Buddhism, but its importance appears gradually to have waned in 
Saivism, which stresses rather the sonic aspect of mantras and of their 
building blocks, the sounds of the syllabary.

1:34-35a ‘If one makes the junction of the brows into the head [of the 
letter], with the pupils of the eyes as the [lower two] dots, this is taught 
to be the letter i; together with the column of the nose [it becomes] the 
long [i]. The letters u and i are [to be discerned in the curly shapes] 
inside the ear.’ 


The earliest type of letter i is simply produced by a cluster of three 
dots (once again, see figure 8 on p.402). In Gupta and post-Gupta 
Northern scripts, one of these dots may become a short line. The line 
may occur at the left, at the right and at the bottom (the most common 
position), but it also may occur at the top (e.g. BÜHLER 1896, Tafel 
IV, column IX), and this presumably is the type that corresponds to 
our prescription, in which the junction of the brows forms the upper 
part of the letter.

‘If one holds both arms upright [and makes] a fist with the right hand, 
[this, taken] together with the head is the letter gha; minus an arm 
(?) [it is] the letter na’ 


The letter gha can indeed be recognised here if one raises both arms 
but keeps them bent at the elbow, and if one discounts the whole body 
below the shoulders (see figure g on p. 411 above). The central prong of 
a Gupta and post-Gupta gha is then recognisable in the head. The left- 
hand upright prong, which has a thickened end, is recognisable in the 
right fist and right forearm of the sadhaka. We may extrapolate from 
this description that whatever is on the sadhaka’s right side typically 
becomes a feature on the left side of the letter as viewed on the page. 
This means that most letters shaped by the sadhaka’s body would not 
be clear to him if he were looking in a mirror, but they would be clear 
to an external observer (such as an uttarasadhaka?). 


Less clear is the letter na. If, taking the letter gha, one were to discount 
the sadhaka’s right arm (both upper arm and forearm), this would 
perhaps give the simple cup shape which, when turned 90° to the 
reader’s right, forms the characteristic shape of a letter na such as it 
appears in ligatures such as rika in Gupta and post-Gupta alphabets.

1:55¢-56 ‘Making the wrist of the right hand into the head [of the letter], 
one should draw together the four fingers and thus make a fist; the 
thumb is to face downwards: the letter na will be produced. 


Here the fist, hanging downwards and with the thumb detached from 
it, is to be arranged so that the back of the hand faces the viewer. The 
fist then gives the thickened knot-like left-hand branch of the Gupta 
na, while the thumb looks like the thinner right-hand branch. 


1:57 “He should put his arms up, placing his arms against his ears, [and 
make] a fist on his right hand: the letter pa will be produced: 


The line produced by the raised lower arms and the top of the head 
will give the distinctive upturned square-cup shape of the old letter 
pa that is typical of Northern scripts from Gupta times up to the end 
of the seventh century and in Southern scripts still later. The fist of 
the right hand produces the knot-like head at the top of the left-hand 
branch of the letter.

1:64ab “Making the line of/from the testicles(?) into the head [of the letter],

In many Southern scripts, and in Northern scripts before 600 AD,

How can these bonds, ॥ 
samsthitah), be bound? Tell me quickly the nature of the bon dc 


this point I have great doubt.’ 
Or perhaps: ‘How do these bonds bind, [and how are they] constituted 
as entities? Or perhaps even: ‘How do these bonds bind, [and how 


are they] arranged in truth?’ 
The speaker-indication has been supplied here because we seem to 
require an introduction to this question about bondage. 


A fundamental tenet of the Saivasiddhanta is that each soul is innately 
all-knowing and all-powerful, but that its nature can only be realised 
by the removal, through a ritual initiation, of bonds that fetter it. 
As mentioned in the introductory pages to this book (pp. 4off), the 
notion that embodied souls are fettered by bonds (pasa) has a long 
history in Saivism. The ancient name ‘Pasupati’, a name of Siva that 
may be translated as ‘Lord of cattle’ or ‘Lord of beasts’, has played a 
role in speculation about bondage because the element pasu is taken 
to refer to beast-like individual souls, who are all bound by bonds 
(paga). Indeed a number of Saiva works begin their presentations of 
doctrine in terms of these three ‘P’s: pati (‘the Lord"), pasu (‘bound 
souls’) and pasa (‘bonds’). And even in tantras in which these three 
do not form by themselves the list of didactic categories (padartha) 
into which the cosmos is divided, they usually form at least a part of 
such lists. 


So what are the bonds by which souls are bound? We have quot- 
ed above the succinct summary of the central problem of bondage 
from SANDERSON’s useful résumé of developed Saiddhantika doctrine 
(1992:285-6, quoted on p.40). Given the centrality of bondage and, 
in particular, of the bond of impurity (mala or anava-mala), to Said- 
dhantika doctrine, one expects to find it expounded in all Saiddhantike 
literature. But, as we began to notice in January 2007, impurity * 
entirely missing from a number of early scriptures of the school.^3? 


The account of bondage in the Nayasütra, as we shall see from Tévara 8 
answer below, is entirely different from those of classical Saiddhantike 
Sources. It first assigns the róle of “binding” in certain particular ways 
to Sadasiva and Tévara, rather implying thereby that the divinities 977 
themselves bound by the obligation to bind, just as the souls they p 


GOODALL et al. 2008:315. 


Translation of the Nayasutra e 
are bound. It then runs through the bonds inflicted by the others 
of the tattvas that we have earlier seen homologised with the nine 
elements of the NAVATMAN. It lists then a number of bodily bonds, and 
bonds inflicted by seven divinities classed as Ganas (1:100f), and is 
concludes with a disparate and catch-all list of constraints experienced 
in life on earth (1:109-111). There is no mention at all of mala, and the 
description of maya leaves one in doubt as to whether it is conceived 
of as “primal matter” or as some sort of “delusion”. 


1:83cd ‘The lord spoke: 
Grace and Occlusion are the two bonds of Sadasiva. 


This is a well-known tag (see apparatus) and it is unclear whether 
this is the source in which it first appeared, for when quoted by Saiva 
authors (see apparatus for quotations by Ramakantha and Tryamba- 
kagambhu) it is taken to be an opponent’s claim that even Sadasiva 
is subject to bonds, whereas here the bonds in question are under 
Sadaáiva's control. But it is possible that this text is its source, that 
it was really intended to mean that the bonds, although they are un- 
der Sadagiva’s control, bind him too with the obligation to use them, 
and that it was later put in the mouths of opponents of Saivism as 
being a statement of Saiva scripture that reveals Siva’s power to be 
circumscribed.

[he] also [bestows] the indestructible condition of being a Gana”. In 
that case we would interpret 1:91d-92b as follows: “Remaining in the 
world in the form of a Linga,?4? I$vara bestows and takes [rewards] 
away.” As for the “indestructability” of being a Gana, perhaps this 
only means that this is a reward that is guaranteed, not that it is 
eternal. One could perhaps understand aksayam and ganatvam to be 
two different rewards. 


As for “the condition of being a Gana”, this is typically a reward 
for lay Saivas (mahesvaras) following a worldly (laukika) religion (cf., 
e.g., Nisvasamukha 1:89, 1:94, 1:115, 1:161, 1:163, 2:18, 3:30, 3:168, 
3:178, 3:192). It is therefore just the sort of a reward that would be 
appropriate for devoted worship, in a laukika fashion, of the linga. 
We shall see below (1:100ff) that the principal Ganas or Ganesvaras 
are seven (not the standard group of eight found in later Siddhanta- 
tantras). Presumably “becoming a Gana” here refers to becoming 
adopted by Siva as part of his train in a similar way to the well-known, 
named Ganas.

1:100b ‘Hear from me the bonds of the [seven divinities known here as the] 
Ganas. 

The following list of seven Ganas is archaic. In most Saiva literature. 
eight Ganas or Gane$varas form one of the circuits around the centra] 
deity in the context of paja. No circuit of eight Ganas features in 
the Nigvasa’s accounts of Siva-worship. Vidyeáa and Hathakusmanda 
do not figure as Ganas elsewhere, and the Nisvasa omits three figures 
who occur in the later standard list, namely Mahakala, Bhrngin ang 
the bull (vrsabha). In a later part of the tantra (Guhyasütra 16:52) 
we find another list of Ganas, again explicitly seven of them and not 
eight, which includes these three (assuming that Kapali stands for 
Mahakala) but omits CandeSa:

It is not clear who Vidyeéa is. There are usually eight Vidyeévaras who

(7:257-8), but not in the earlier sütras of this text. The most impor- 
tant of them is Ananta, and it is possible therefore that 0107०69 here 
means Ananta, who is not usually classed as a Gana.

His being elephant-faced is not mentioned, however, in either place.

that discusses aiva chapters that have been added to the old Skan-

to be early (2004:21-2). The first is the consistent use of the name 
Vinayaka, never ganeSa or gane$vara, for the latter are invariably not 
proper names but terms of rank in the old Skandapurana, just as they 
are frequently are in other early Saiva works, such as the Nisvasa-

name Vinayaka, with the class of possession-demons called vinayakas, 
and not with his now familiar róle of removing obstacles (vighnavina- 
yaka). We might therefore expect to find here only the name Vinayaka 
used, not Ganapati or, as in Nayasütra 4:104 below, VighneSa. But 
other comparably early allusions to an elephant-faced Ganapati can 
in fact be found, such as the second of Bana's introductory verses 
to the fourth ucchvasa of the Harsacarita, to which TORZSOK refers 
(2004:22, fn. 22), in which the name used is Ganadhipa and the trope 
concerns his tusk. The Amarakośa also catalogues names that allude 
to his being elephant-faced, that suggest a fairly developed mytholo- 
gy, that reveal an association with the removal of obstacles and that 
include the “rank” Ganadhipa (1.1:39):

2:19cd ‘..[knowledge (?) of] cosmic hierarchy and Saiva initiation— [n 
these] may be obtained through [knowledge (?) of] these tattvas? 


This might appear to allude to some form of tattvadiksa, but there 
is none described in the text. Alternatively, this may be intended to 
mean only that an initiating guru requires true knowledge of the tatt- 
vas in order correctly to understand the prakriya (into which the tatt- 
vas are embedded) and in order thereby to be able to perform effective 
initiation (cf. the knowledge required of the alphabet, matrka, in the 
previous chapter). (Another less likely possibility is that the tattvas, 
since they have been homologised with elements of the NAVATMAN, a 
crucial mantra, are instruments in the performance of initiation.)

2:54-56b ‘The subtle element of smell [residing in the sense of smell] gras 
smell through the tip of the nose. The subtle element of taste तीन 
in the tongue grasps taste. The subtle element of form [residing in the 
sense of sight] grasps form, when [form is] presented [to the perceiver] 
(upagatam), through the eyes. The subtle element of touch residing 
in the skin, grasps touch. The subtle element of sound xus when it 
becomes sound in the faculty of the ear (Srotragabdatvam agatah): 


As far as we are aware, this notion that the tanmatras residing in 
the faculties (or in the places in the body in which those faculties 
are concentrated, such as the nose) are responsible for perceiving the 
same tanmatras, residing as gunas in external objects, is not a notion 
that known figures among the Sankhyas have propounded. Ksema- 
raja defends this rather odd view in his Svacchandatantroddyota (ad 
12:33-35b). 

Note that these sentences have been rephrased, in order to obviate the 
(metrical) need for pratipadikas in the Svacchanda (12:33ff). In one 
case, spar$atanmatra, the use of the pratipadika only obeys the metre 
if one treats the following ligature (spa) as not making the previous 
syllable long. It is possible that jihvayam is a corruption of jihvaya, a 
metrically required lengthened form of the instrumental jihvaya. For 
the expression Srotrasabdatvam agatam, cf. the Nepalese reading of 
the previous line in the Svacchanda (12:34cd). 


2:56cd "The elements have as their subtle properties the subtle elements 
in due order from the beginning" 


It is uncertain to us whether this is what the text really means. Ksema- 
raja’s interpretation of this line, in which he reads prakrtikramat, takes 
this as a statement to the effect that the above lines were teaching a 
subtle, which is to say generally unknown, property of the tanmatras 
as residing in the indriyas. But it is not clear that this is what the 
text was originally meant to express.

2:61c-63b ‘I have taught [you] the properties of ahankara; hear from me 
the properties of the buddhi: piety (dharmam), knowledge (jrianam), 
dispassion (vairagyam), and control (ai$varyam) as the fourth, and 
impiety, nescience, lack of dispassion and lack of control. This [bud- 
dhi) binds [thus] in seven ways [viz. through seven of the above eight 
properties], but liberates through the disposition that is knowledge 
(jranabhavena). 
Usually all four of the bhavas, that is to say the positive properties 
of the buddhi, are placed on an equal footing (for the workings of 
the buddhidharmas, see below and cf., e.g., Parakhya 4:74-90). The 
emphasis on jfiana here might seem to suggest a stronger emphasis 
on gnosis than is typical of the later Saivasiddhanta, but it becomes 
clear in 2:69—70 below that the redactor is thinking of the Sankhyas' 
discrimination of purusa and prakrti leading to kaivalya. 


2:63cd "The intellect (buddhih), through discrimination, makes and alters: 


Discrimination (adhyavasaya) is well known to be the responsibili- 
ty of the buddhi (e.g. in Sarikhyakarika 23), but it is not clear here 
what it “makes” and what it “alters” (karoti vikaroti ca); perhaps it 
changes the moods of the person? The pāda is a not particularly com- 
mon cliché, found, for example, in Mahābhārata 3-31:33d; Bhagavata- 
gurang nid Brahmandapurana 3.2:281d; Kürmapurüna 1-4-54d and 
1.11:224d.

N here transmits prakrti, a prātipadika, which, although we have not

version of the corresponding unit in the Svacchanda (12:64cd) has ob- 
viated the difficulty by reformulating: tasya dharmam pravaksyami 
sattvarajastamobhidham.

3:42-44a ‘By meditating on the frontal face, which is a yellow Ardhanariéa 
with three eyes and matted locks, he obtains the merit of fone who 
lives on nothing but the air], and of ten thousand horse-sacrifices, and 
the universe will come under his thrall; he will stride [about in it] and 
be powerful, within six months, there is no doubt? 


Here begins a visualisation of each of the faces of I$vara in turn, this 
being now the level of 1i$varatattva (not of sadasivatattva), beginning 
in the East. As well as our notes below, the reader may refer to 
TORZSOK 2013:41-45 for a discussion of this passage. 


We may note that the name SadaSiva is not used here, that there 
is no correlation explicitly established between each face and a giv- 
en brahmamantra, and that it is possible that only four rather than 
five faces are intended. After four faces have been described, verses 
3:52-53 appear to give a description of the body, rather than the face, 
of a figure placed on top of the four-faced head. In short, this is not an 
iconographical account of a Sadasiva—indeed we find no iconography 
of Sadagiva in the NiSvaso—but it reflects a stage in the evolution of 
the iconography of Sadasiva, and it appears to have been interpreted as 
an account of the iconography of Sadasiva by transmitters of the Sva- 
cchanda, who have at some point replaced Ardhanariga as the Eastern 
“face” with Narega, intended as a synonym of Tatpurusa (12:125¢d): 
the Nepalese manuscript we have collated retains Ardhanarisa, but in 
the KSTS we find kunkumabham ca naresam trinetram tu jatadharam, 
and Ksemaraja comments: ardhanarigam ity apapathah, “Ardhanarisa 
is a wrong reading”.

3:64 “When Sadasiva has been understood, with His eight divisions, with 
respect to [viz. "in"?] the day, night, the semesters, through (?) the 
movement from South to North [at the solstices], in the equinoctial 
point (?), He is liberatory. 


Note that the structure here has been expanded and altered both in 
the Nepalese and Kashmirian texts of the Svacchanda (Appendix II, 
12:147-8). Our text, however, is difficult to construe since the case- 
endings do not mark the intended structure of the sentence. Presum- 
ably the verse refers to Sadasiva as the root-mantra of the tantra (the 
eight divisions of which are taught in Mulasitra 6) being meditated 
upon as fused with the breath present in different parts of the micro- 
cosmic yogic body homologised with the macrocosm. Day and night, 
therefore, refer to the ingoing and outgoing breaths (cf. Uttarasutra 
5:37), and they are mentioned to indicate that while breathing in one 
should focus on a mantra-form of Sadasiva. The uninflected form visu- 
va, used to fit the metrical cadence, we assume to be a locative. This 
“equinox” in the body we take to be the moment when the soul-breath, 
meditated upon as fused with the mantra, is in a place of rest between 
the left and right tubes. Whether there is or is not supposed to bea 
central tube here is not clear (cf. Uttarasiitra 5:38 and annotation).

The interpretation of visuddhika (and Suddha [for "Suddha?] in amái- 
rasuddha) to refer to the “solution” of a symbol or code is uncertain; 
such a usage is typical of Buddhist commentarial literature (see SFER- 
RA 1999) and may be unparalleled in early Saiva sources. Alterna- 
tively, one could split maya from visuddhika and take the latter as an 
adjective meaning “pure 1.6. without a following vowel]”. As for the 
element Suddha, that too could be understood as not forming part of 
a compound: “pure [i.e. without a preceding vowel]” Or it could per- 
haps instead be intended to qualify vidya and to distinguish it from 
the non-pure vidya, namely the tattva of Uttarasutra 1:11. Confus- 
ingly, that same tattva came later to be known as Suddhavidyatattva 
to distinguish it from the yet lower vidyatattva among the karicukas. 
The lower vidya among the kaficukas is absent, however, in the earliest 
sutras in the Nisvasa, and when it does make its appearance ( Guhya- 
sutra 7:236) the Ni$vasa's original vidyatattva becomes distinguished 
with the label mahavidya (7:249).

4:46—7 ‘One who quests after knowledge is not worth a sixteenth part of

We assume that mahanidrà is an irregularly formed ablative (maha- 
nidrat) that has been truncated by the loss of its final consonant. ak- 
lesat siddhimoksadah is a rare cliché: we find it as Uttarasutra 5:46b 
(and Satikakalottara 101b, copied from the Uttarasütra). In this rank- 
ing of yoga above knowledge we see perhaps an adumbration of the 
as yet unattested notion that scripture is devoted to the four topics 
(pada) of jñāna, yoga, carya and kriya.

4:67 “The goddess spoke: 


The whole universe of moving and non-moving beings has arisen from 
the power of Siva, and I have heard it at length up to the eleventh? 


We suppose that "the eleventh" may refer to the nine tattvas together 
with Sakti and niskala/ niralamba. This would then bea reference back 
to the teaching of eleven tattvas making up the universe correlated 
with eleven elements in the NAVATMAN: Uttarasitra 131-12. 


4:68 ‘[I have also heard] the letters that are the [yogic] focus-points [using 
which one can meditate] on the tattvas, [and] differentiation of [the 
layers] of the cosmography [required for the performance of] diksa, 
and meditation [on those] separately [viz. in chapters 2 and 3], and 
also a [state of mental awareness in which everything has the] same 
flavour [as Siva] (samarasam) has been described? 


In this interpretation aksaras tattvalaksah alludes to the fact that the 
letters of the NAVATMAN have been homologised with the tattvas in the 
beginning of the Uttarasutra. But we could take that teaching to be 
alluded to only by the word aksarah and understand tattvalaksah (for 
tattvalaksyani) to refer to the mental focus-points using which one can 
meditate on the tattvas. These are referred to and discussed in Uttara- 
sutra 5:6 and 5:10ff. For the “same-flavour” awareness, see 4:55 and 
surrounding verses above. One could perhaps interpret diksaprakriya- 
bhedanam to mean: “and the penetration of [the various successive 
layers of] the cosmos through initiation"

to Susumna is uncertain. One could instead have split sugumpnà p adike

a name for the northern tube of the yogic body (not the central one): 
but this seems unlikely to be intended here. In the cosmography i 
die Guhyasütra (7:293-5), however, Susumna is a subtle goddess d 
situated above nada and having the shape of a lotus-fibre.

4:80-82b ‘If someone engaged in yoga, thoroughly controlled, meditates 
[upon the Sivacakra] for one month, supernatural power [associated 
with all levels up to that] of prakrti will arise [for him]; in two months 
however, supernatural power [associated with all levels up to that of 
the tattva] of purusa [will arise]. The [eight levels of] power associated 
with niyati, kala, maya, vidya, 1$vara, bindu, the [four] kalas and with 
Sakti are attained each with one [extra] month ... eight...’ 


It is possible that the scribe finished copying early on this first line 
of the folio, and that we are therefore missing no more than the end 
of this half-line, in which case some notion such as possessing eight- 
fold ai$varya might have been expressed, for instance with a pada 
such as astaisvaryasamanvitah. Also conceivable, however, is that a 
full further half-line is missing, which could mean that we had a list 
of eight properties culminating in sarvajnah etc. (of 4:82cd below). 
But one could consider that we have already had eight levels of siddhi 
listed (if one leaves off prakrti and purusa) and all that may be partly 
missing is an expression of the idea that the eight above-listed types 
may be attained within eight months. How this would be phrased is 
uncertain.

homologised in the following verse? But then how is it referred to by 
the expression paficavarnatribhinnakah? And, if it is it not referred

shall see in the following verses that A, U and M are subdivided into 
short, long and prolated forms, which could conceivably be what the 
element tribhinna alludes to, but this would not help us to arrive at 8 
tally of eight matras.

as a state that underlies all three other pranayamas.

This verse of the Nisvasa may, however, be the earliest Passage in 
which it is assigned the name Suprasanta/ Prasanta. This fourth phase 
referred to as Prasanta, is also mentioned in Siddhayogesvarimata "isa 
(see TORZSOK 1999*:132), where it is associated with the seed Sylla 
ble of Para. A detailed explanation is given in the Tantraloka and 
Tantrülokaviveka (17:87ff). As Yuko YOKOCHI has observed to us 
again in her reader’s report, pranayama is also said to be fourfold 
in the old Skandapurana 179:37b (pranayamam caturvidham), but no 
name appears there for the fourth phase. 


In some Buddhist tantric literature this fourth pranayama is referred 
to as prasantaka, e.g. Hevajratantra 1.xi.3 (patana recakenaiva kumb- 
hakena vaéikaret/ pürakenaiva tv akrstih prasantakena stambhana), 
Samvarodayatantra 19:30, and in the auto-commentary on Vagigvara- 
kirti's eleventh-century Tattvaratnavaloka, which refers to Sankhyas 
and Saivas as the source of the information.25 


James MALLINSON, in a letter of 2.viii.2011, has commented that the 
fourth pranayama may be what is called kevalakumbhaka “in a num- 
ber of early hatha texts, including the Dattatreyayogasastra, Goraksa- 
Sataka, Vasisthasamhita (its verses on it are also found in the Yoga- 
yajnavalkya) and the Hathapradipika compilation (using verses from 
all the aforementioned texts)" The description of kevalakumbhaka, 
which is apparently something that can be performed after years of 
practice, is to be found described in verses 2:71-4 of the last named 
work.

control practices in addition to püraka, recaka and kumbhaka, namely 
pratyahara, Santa, uttara and adhara (5:5). Among these, Santa is &
